title: Write the spec in exact numbers, not descriptive words
hypothesis: If we replace words like centered or about with exact measurements in the spec, then wrong or inconsistent batches drop because the factory has no open point left to guess on.

signal.check: The current spec has words like centered, about, similar or standard instead of numbers, or a reorder arrived a different shade, weight or size than the PDP photo.

expected_effect.size: removes the open points that made one factory ship a batch in 3 shades and 2 fabric weights from one spec

risk.note: Rewriting a document only; no supplier commitment changes.

prerequisites: Product drawings or reference photos
The current spec or tech pack
steps: List every dimension, placement and colour reference in the current spec.
Mark every word that is not a number, such as centered, about or standard.
Replace each with an exact measurement, position or Pantone code.
Check the new spec against the approved sample or PDP photos for a match.
Save the corrected spec as a new version and send it before the next factory message.

test.method: Compare the next sample or batch to the corrected spec line by line.
test.measure: Spec mismatches per batch, return rate for not as described
test.read_point: On the first sample after the rewrite, then the first full shipment

title: Add a tolerance band to every measurement in the spec
hypothesis: If we write an acceptable tolerance next to every exact measurement, then a factory decision on a borderline unit is judged against a written line, not guessed, so fewer disputed units reach QC.

signal.check: The spec has exact numbers but no plus-or-minus tolerance, so QC has no written line for a borderline unit.

risk.note: Documentation change only.

prerequisites: A spec with exact measurements (COG-001)
steps: Take each measurement, placement and colour line in the spec.
Set an acceptable tolerance the brand will accept for each one.
Add the tolerance next to the target number in the spec.
Share the tolerance list with the factory and the inspector.

test.method: Track how many QC disputes cite a measurement with no tolerance versus one with a tolerance.
test.measure: Disputed units per shipment
test.read_point: After the next 2 pre-shipment inspections

title: Write one versioned tech pack per SKU
hypothesis: If every SKU has one dated tech pack with drawings, materials, measurements, colourways and packaging, then every quote, sample and PO cite the same version, so drift between them stops.

signal.check: A listed SKU's only spec is a chat thread with the factory, or no version number appears on the quote, sample log and PO.

risk.note: A living document; low cost to build, about $200 if outsourced.

prerequisites: Product drawings or photos
Approved reference sample if one exists
steps: Create one document per SKU with drawings from every angle, materials and finishes with GSM, trims and hardware.
Add measurements for every size and variant, colourways with Pantone codes, and label, packaging and care instructions.
Add the product name, version number and date.
If nobody in-house can draw it, brief a product designer, about $200 on Upwork.
Store the pack in the brand's own system, not only at the factory, and give it a version number.
Cite this version on every quote, sample log and purchase order.

test.method: Check whether the version number on the PO draft matches the pack sent to the factory.
test.measure: Version match rate across quote, sample and PO
test.read_point: On the next PO for this SKU

title: Build a component-level bill of materials for the hero SKU
hypothesis: If we break the factory quote into components, sub-supplier, lead time, country, terms, and labor and overhead as separate lines, then we can see where the negotiating room and the risk actually sit, because a lump factory cost hides both.
does_not_apply_when: A first small test order can run on the tech pack alone.

signal.check: An invoice or quote shows one factory cost line and a price, terms or tariff negotiation is coming up.

expected_effect.size: unknown, depends on where the room is once the lines are visible

risk.note: Analysis only; some suppliers may resist sharing labor and overhead lines.

prerequisites: A current factory quote or invoice
A supplier relationship with some rapport
steps: List every physical component of the finished unit plus retail packaging as its own line.
For each line capture component cost, sub-supplier, lead time, country of origin, payment terms.
Split labor and overhead into their own lines instead of one factory cost figure.
Mark any line the supplier will not share as unavailable and note who to ask again later.
Check that the lines sum to the factory quote within an explained gap.

test.method: Compare the summed BOM lines against the factory's quoted price.
test.measure: Variance between BOM sum and quoted price
test.read_point: As soon as the BOM is built, then again at the next quote

title: Physically verify BOM lines and PDP material claims with the supplier
hypothesis: If we take the product apart with the supplier and test every PDP material claim, then a claim like organic cotton or solid gold is provable, because an unproven claim is a refund and a policy risk.

signal.check: A PDP claim about material, such as organic cotton or solid gold, has never been tested or certified against a BOM line.

risk.note: A verification step; no product change.

prerequisites: A BOM (COG-004)
A supplier willing to disassemble a sample unit
steps: List every PDP claim about the product's materials.
Ask the supplier to disassemble a unit and show the component behind each claim.
Test or request certification for bought-in components like diamonds, gold, zippers or chipsets.
Map the sub-vendor layer under the factory for each bought-in part.
Mark any claim that cannot be proven and remove or soften it on the PDP.

test.method: Track PDP claims with a mapped, tested or certified BOM line versus claims with none.
test.measure: Share of PDP material claims backed by a tested BOM line
test.read_point: Before the next PDP copy update

title: Send a physical reference sample with the tech pack to a new factory
hypothesis: If we send a physical reference item plus written specs to a candidate factory, then the sample it returns is judged against a real object, not a description, because quality words alone leave room to misread.
does_not_apply_when: No authorised reference item exists yet, or the reference is another brand's branded product with no IP check done.

signal.check: A well-reviewed SKU needs a second or cheaper factory, or a new SKU is modelled on a unit the brand already owns.

risk.note: Sending a branded reference item without an IP check risks a design or trademark issue.

prerequisites: An owned or authorised reference item
Written specs (materials, dimensions, tolerances)
steps: Confirm the reference item is the brand's own or has a clear IP check if modelled on another brand's product.
Send the exact item to the candidate factory along with written specs.
Ask the factory to replicate it on the attributes reviews praise most.
Compare the returned sample against the reference side by side and record deviations.

test.method: Score the sample against the reference on the top review-praised attributes.
test.measure: Deviation count per attribute
test.read_point: On receipt of the first sample from this factory

title: Store tech packs and source files in the brand's own system
hypothesis: If tech packs, artwork and source files live in the brand's own drive and not only at the factory, then a supplier switch or a second factory can start from an existing file, because rebuilding from zero costs weeks.

signal.check: The current tech pack, artwork or source files exist only in the factory's system, not the brand's own storage.

risk.note: A copy step; no change to the current supplier relationship.

prerequisites: A final supplier chosen
steps: Ask the current supplier for the current tech pack, artwork and any source files.
Save every file in the brand's own drive with the SKU name and version.
Check that the files open and match the version cited on the last PO.
Repeat for every SKU at volume, and note where a manufacturing agreement or trademark should be registered.

test.method: Try opening every key SKU's files from the brand's own storage without contacting the factory.
test.measure: Share of SKUs whose files open from the brand's own system
test.read_point: Once per quarter

title: Use the BOM to test an entry or premium version of a SKU
hypothesis: If we build a cheaper or premium input tier as its own SKU using the BOM's cost gaps, then a new price point can be tested honestly, because the price gap can be checked against a real cost gap instead of guessed.

signal.check: The collection page shows one SKU at one price point with no tested entry or premium tier.

risk.note: A new SKU test; can be discontinued if it underperforms.

prerequisites: A component-level BOM (COG-004)
steps: Review the BOM for a component that has a cheaper or premium substitute.
Price the substitute component and compute the new landed cost.
Set a test price for the new tier based on the real cost gap, not a guess.
List it as its own SKU and route a small share of traffic to it.
Compare margin and sell-through against the original SKU.

test.method: Run the new tier alongside the original SKU for a set period.
test.measure: AOV, gross margin, sell-through of the new tier versus the original
test.read_point: After the tier reaches a stable sample of orders, at least 4 weeks

title: Quote retail packaging as its own line in the BOM
hypothesis: If packaging gets its own quote and BOM line instead of sitting inside factory cost, then packaging cost becomes visible and negotiable, because a lump line hides how much of it is markup.

signal.check: Packaging cost sits inside a single factory cost line with no separate quote.

expected_effect.size: one operator reports cutting packaging cost more than 50% once it became its own line

risk.note: A quoting change; packaging quality should still be checked against the reference sample.

prerequisites: A BOM (COG-004)
steps: Ask the factory or a packaging supplier for a standalone packaging quote per unit.
Add it as its own line in the BOM, separate from factory cost.
Check the new carton size and weight against the freight calculation, since packaging changes ship weight.
Compare the standalone quote against what packaging currently costs inside the lump line.

test.method: Compare the old bundled packaging estimate to the new standalone quote.
test.measure: Packaging cost per unit before and after
test.read_point: On the next packaging quote request

title: Build the missing BOM before any negotiation on a takeover or new client
hypothesis: If a BOM does not exist when a brand is acquired or onboarded, then building it becomes the first task before any cost-down call, because negotiating without one means negotiating blind.

signal.check: No BOM exists for the brand's SKUs at the start of an acquisition, onboarding or first audit.

risk.note: A build task; delays negotiation slightly but avoids negotiating without data.

prerequisites: Access to existing invoices and supplier contacts
steps: Confirm whether a BOM exists for the hero SKU and other key SKUs.
If none exists, run COG-004 to build it before any cost-down conversation.
Read the country-of-origin and supplier columns for concentration exposure.
Ask when COGS on the SKU last went down; treat never as a sign there is room.

test.method: Track whether a negotiation happens before or after the BOM exists.
test.measure: BOM completeness at first negotiation
test.read_point: Before the first cost-down call on a new or acquired brand

title: Ask when COGS last declined on a mature SKU
hypothesis: If we ask when a mature SKU's cost last went down, then an answer of never signals real negotiating room, because a supplier relationship with no cost movement over years has not been tested.

signal.check: A SKU has sold for a year or more with no recorded cost-down or price-break review.

risk.note: A question to ask; no commitment made.

prerequisites: A BOM or at least cost history per SKU
steps: Pull the cost history for each mature SKU.
Note the date of the last cost change, up or down.
Flag any SKU with no cost-down in over a year as a negotiation candidate.
Add it to the next cost-down or BOM review conversation.

test.method: Track SKUs flagged this way and whether a negotiation follows.
test.measure: Number of SKUs with a cost review started after the flag
test.read_point: Within one quarter of the flag

title: Give the hero SKU a full BOM and a vetted backup factory first
hypothesis: If the SKU carrying most of paid spend gets a full BOM and a vetted backup factory before the rest of the catalogue, then a supply failure there is caught early, because that SKU does the most damage if it stocks out or its cost is wrong.
does_not_apply_when: Even coverage across many SKUs with no single dominant seller.

signal.check: One or a few SKUs carry most of paid spend and orders, but sourcing effort is spread evenly across the catalogue.

risk.note: A prioritisation choice, not a new commitment.

prerequisites: Ad spend or order share per SKU
steps: Rank SKUs by share of paid spend and orders.
Confirm the top SKU has a full component BOM (COG-004).
Confirm the top SKU has at least one vetted backup factory with a passed sample.
Only then extend the same work to the rest of the catalogue.

test.method: Check BOM and backup status for the hero SKU versus the rest of the catalogue.
test.measure: Coverage of BOM and backup factory by SKU rank
test.read_point: Before the next sourcing review

title: Use Alibaba for research and shortlisting, not the final pick, on an ad-spend SKU
hypothesis: If a filtered Alibaba search is treated as a research step and not the final factory choice for an ad-spend SKU, then the store avoids a decent-but-not-best factory, because the best factories come from a curated shortlist, not a filter.
does_not_apply_when: A low-volume or test SKU, where a filtered search is a fair floor.

signal.check: A new SKU or category has no supplier yet, or the last supplier came from the first search result.

risk.note: Extends the search timeline; low risk otherwise.

prerequisites: A locked spec (COG-001)
steps: Use Alibaba to research price, materials and MOQ range for the category.
Build a shortlist of candidates rather than picking the first strong listing.
For a hero SKU or one with planned ad spend, keep vetting past the filtered list.
For a low-volume or test SKU, a filtered search result is an acceptable floor.
Record why each factory was shortlisted.

test.method: Compare defect rate and on-time rate of filtered-search suppliers versus fully vetted ones over time.
test.measure: Defect rate, on-time ship rate by sourcing method
test.read_point: After the first 2 shipments from each supplier

title: Message 10 to 15 factories and filter to verified suppliers with Trade Assurance
hypothesis: If we message at least 10 to 15 candidate factories and filter to verified, Trade Assurance suppliers, then the shortlist starts from a wide, protected pool, because a launch date fixed against one unvetted factory risks a sold-out PDP.

signal.check: A launch date or ad budget is set against a single unvetted factory with no shortlist built.

risk.note: Outreach only; no commitment made.

prerequisites: A locked spec (COG-001)
steps: Search Alibaba for the exact product type.
Filter to verified suppliers and Trade Assurance.
Message at least 10 to 15 candidates with the spec version and a quote request.
Record years active, export markets and listed certifications for each responder.

test.method: Count candidates that pass this first filter before moving to video calls.
test.measure: Number of qualified candidates per search
test.read_point: Once outreach responses come back, typically within a week

title: Video-call the shortlist to inspect the facility before trusting it
hypothesis: If we video-call every shortlisted factory and ask to see the facility or sample products, then a candidate operating from a home or giving vague answers is dropped early, because a dropped factory late leaves the PDP sold out.

signal.check: A candidate has only exchanged text messages, with no video call or facility view before a launch date is set.

risk.note: A screening step.

prerequisites: A shortlist from outreach (COG-014)
steps: Schedule a video call with each responding candidate.
Ask to see the facility, or sample products already made.
Drop candidates with vague answers, poor communication, or signs of a home setup.
Record the call outcome next to the candidate on the shortlist.

test.method: Track how many candidates are dropped at this stage versus later, after commitment.
test.measure: Drop rate at video call versus drop rate after sample or PO
test.read_point: After each new supplier search

title: Require ISO or BSCI certification and drop a refusal
hypothesis: If we request ISO or BSCI certificates from every shortlisted factory and treat a refusal as a drop, then the store avoids a supplier that will not stand behind its own claims, because a refusal is itself a red flag.

signal.check: A shortlisted factory has not provided certificates, or years active and export markets are unconfirmed.

risk.note: A documentation request.

prerequisites: A shortlist that passed the video call (COG-015)
steps: Request ISO or BSCI certificates from each remaining candidate.
Verify years active and export markets against the certificate.
Drop any candidate that refuses or cannot produce a certificate.
Record certificate status on the shortlist record.

test.method: Track whether certified suppliers show fewer defects or disputes than uncertified ones over time.
test.measure: Defect rate and dispute count by certification status
test.read_point: After the first shipment from a newly certified supplier

title: Keep at least one vetted backup factory for every SKU carrying ad spend
hypothesis: If a core SKU with ad spend or a promo date has a second factory already vetted with a passed sample, then a failure at the main factory does not stop the SKU from shipping, because a backup that exists only as a claim gives no real protection.

signal.check: A core SKU with ad spend has one factory and no tested backup on file.

risk.note: A vetting cost, usually a sample fee, for a factory that may never be used.

prerequisites: A shortlist with at least 2 vetted candidates
steps: Identify every core SKU that carries meaningful ad spend or a promo date.
Confirm a second factory exists in the shortlist for that SKU.
Run that backup through the sample stage (COG-025 to COG-029) before it is needed.
Mark the backup as current on the supplier record, with the date it was last tested.

test.method: Check whether every ad-spend SKU has a backup with a passed sample on file.
test.measure: Share of ad-spend SKUs with a current, tested backup
test.read_point: Before setting any launch or promo date

title: Get a direct contact channel with every supplier at first contact
hypothesis: If we get a WhatsApp, WeChat or email contact with every supplier at first contact, then a PO due the week a supplier goes dark on platform chat still has a way through, because platform chat alone can go silent with no notice.

signal.check: A supplier is reachable only through platform chat, with no direct channel on file.

risk.note: A contact request; refusal is itself useful information.

steps: At first contact with any new supplier, ask for a direct channel: WhatsApp, WeChat or email.
Record the direct contact on the supplier record alongside the platform chat.
Treat a refusal to share one as a diligence flag on the shortlist.

test.method: Track how many active suppliers have a direct channel on file.
test.measure: Share of active suppliers with a recorded direct contact
test.read_point: Quarterly supplier record review

title: Vet a sourcing agent with a sample, a direct channel and references before using them
hypothesis: If a sourcing agent is only used after a sample from their factory, a direct channel and references from similar-volume brands, then volume is not routed through an unvetted middle layer, because an agent with none of these has no proof behind their claims.
does_not_apply_when: The store negotiates directly with factories and has no need for an agent.

signal.check: A trading-company quote looks inflated with no explanation, or a SKU needs custom tooling and an agent is being considered with none of the 3 checks done.

risk.note: Routing volume through an unvetted agent risks quality and payment control.

prerequisites: A quote gap that needs explaining, or a customisation need
steps: Ask the candidate agent for a physical sample from their factory.
Get a direct contact channel with the agent, separate from any platform chat.
Ask for references from brands at a similar volume.
Do not route any volume through the agent until all 3 are on file.

test.method: Track whether all 3 checks are complete before the first order through an agent.
test.measure: Share of agent relationships with all 3 checks on file
test.read_point: Before the first order placed through any agent

title: Never buy or open a factory without a specific unmet quality gap
hypothesis: If factory ownership is only considered when a specific, unmet engineering or quality gap exists that no vetted factory can close, then the store avoids a capital-heavy move made on cost alone, because most impulse factory purchases the sources describe failed.

signal.check: A founder is considering buying or opening a factory, and the trigger is cost, not a specific unmet quality gap.

risk.note: A decision check, not an action with its own risk.

steps: Write down the specific engineering or quality gap driving the idea.
Confirm at least 2 vetted factories have failed to close that gap through samples.
If the trigger is cost alone, stop and pursue a cost-down negotiation instead.
Only proceed if someone is prepared to be on site.

test.method: Review the written gap and the 2-factory-failure evidence before any capital commitment.
test.measure: Whether the gap and evidence exist in writing
test.read_point: Before any factory purchase or lease decision

title: Get a factory-direct or manufacturer quote alongside any intermediary's
hypothesis: If we get a factory-direct quote for any product currently bought through a distributor or trading company, then the margin gap the intermediary charges becomes visible, because a distributor's price can carry a large hidden markup.

signal.check: A product is bought through a domestic distributor or trading company with no factory-direct quote on file.

expected_effect.size: one swag example showed about 30% below the domestic price at factory-direct

risk.note: A quote request only; keep the intermediary relationship until a switch is decided.

prerequisites: The category or product bought through an intermediary today
steps: Identify the SKU currently bought through a domestic distributor or trading company.
Request a factory-direct or manufacturer quote on the same spec and quantity.
Compute the landed cost for the factory-direct option (F6).
Compare it against the current intermediary price on identical terms.
Decide whether the gap justifies a switch, a test order, or a renegotiation with the intermediary.

test.method: Compare landed cost of the factory-direct quote against the current intermediary price.
test.measure: Cost gap percentage between intermediary and factory-direct
test.read_point: Once the factory-direct quote is in hand

title: Request a structured quote and compare suppliers only on identical terms
hypothesis: If every supplier is asked for the same fields, unit cost, MOQ, lead time, packaging, terms, incoterm and validity, then quotes can be compared fairly, because a single price number with no terms gives no real comparison or leverage.

signal.check: A supplier answered a price question with one number and no MOQ, lead time, packaging or terms attached.

risk.note: A request format change only.

prerequisites: A locked spec version (COG-003)
A shortlist of suppliers
steps: Send every shortlisted factory the same spec version.
Ask together for unit cost per SKU and variant, MOQ, production lead time, packaging details and payment terms.
Ask for incoterm and quote validity date.
Reject any quote missing a field and ask again before comparing.

test.method: Check that every supplier's quote has all required fields filled at the same quantity and incoterm.
test.measure: Share of quotes with all fields complete
test.read_point: Before building the quote comparison table

title: Request quotes at several volume tiers and compare cash and cover, not just price
hypothesis: If quotes are requested at 3 or more quantity tiers and shown side by side with cash locked and days of cover, then the owner sees what a discount costs in cash, because the lowest unit price is not always the best tier once cash lock-up is counted.

signal.check: A bulk order is being considered from a single quoted quantity, with no tier comparison or cash-lock view.

expected_effect.size: one case saw unit price fall from about $7.80 to $2.00 across tiers, with cash lock rising sharply at the deepest tier

risk.note: An analysis step; the risk sits in which tier is chosen, not in requesting quotes.

prerequisites: A structured quote request (COG-022)
A forwarder quote per tier
The current daily sales velocity
steps: Post an RFQ or ask each supplier for 3 or more quantity tiers.
Compute landed cost per unit for each tier (F6).
Compute cash at deposit, cash total and days of cover for each tier (F8).
Present every tier side by side and mark the tier the price favours versus the tier cash favours.

test.method: Show the tier table to the owner before any bulk order is placed.
test.measure: Cash locked and days of cover per tier
test.read_point: Before choosing a tier on any bulk PO

title: Treat the first quote as an opening position, not the final price
hypothesis: If the first quote received is treated as an opening position and negotiated before committing volume, then unit cost drops before a bulk order locks it in, because one recorded case saved about $3,500 per order at their volume by negotiating first.

signal.check: A quote is about to be accepted as final with no counter-offer or backup quote used.

expected_effect.size: one case moved from $6.00 to $4.80 per unit, about $3,500 saved per order

risk.note: A negotiation step; pushing too hard without a real backup can strain the relationship.

prerequisites: A structured quote (COG-022)
Ideally a backup quote (COG-017) on identical terms
steps: Record the opening quote with its date and terms.
Use the backup quote, if one exists, as a reference point in the counter.
Ask for a lower price or better terms before committing any volume.
Record both the opening and the accepted price.

test.method: Track opening price versus accepted price on every bulk quote.
test.measure: Price movement between opening and accepted quote
test.read_point: After each negotiation closes

title: Use landed cost per unit, not the factory quote, as the pricing decision number
hypothesis: If every pricing, ad-spend and go or no-go decision cites landed cost per unit instead of the ex-factory price, then a decision is not made on a margin that looks better than it is, because freight, duty, insurance and fulfilment can turn an assumed 60% margin into an actual 20%.

signal.check: A PDP price, ad budget or supplier decision cites the ex-factory quote with no landed cost calculation behind it.

expected_effect.size: one case moved from about 60% assumed margin to about 20% actual after landed cost lines were added

risk.note: A calculation step; the risk is proceeding without it, not doing it.

prerequisites: Freight quote
Duty rate or paid amount
Insurance, inbound handling and inspection cost per unit
steps: Compute landed cost per unit before setting any price, ad budget or supplier decision (F6).
Include factory price, freight share, duty and tax paid, insurance, inbound handling, packaging and inspection cost.
Run this before manufacturing starts, not after production is underway.
Cite the landed cost number, with its date, on every such decision.

test.method: Compare the ex-factory price against the computed landed cost for each SKU.
test.measure: Gap between ex-factory price and landed cost as a percentage
test.read_point: Before the first PO for any new SKU

title: Confirm a SKU's margin is healthy on its own sell-through before a bulk order
hypothesis: If a bulk order is only placed after the SKU's own sell-through shows a healthy contribution margin, then the store avoids locking cash into a SKU that cannot fund the ad spend needed to sell it, because a thin margin cannot cover the cash lock-up and defect risk of a deep volume tier.

signal.check: A bulk PO is planned on a SKU whose margin has not been confirmed from its own sell-through, only from a forecast.

risk.note: A bulk order placed on a thin margin without this check can lock cash into unsold or unprofitable stock.

prerequisites: Landed cost per unit (COG-025)
Actual sell-through data for the SKU
steps: Pull actual sell-through and contribution margin for the SKU from its own sales history.
Compare against the store's minimum margin threshold before scaling.
If the margin is thin, hold the bulk order and address cost or price first.
Only proceed to the volume tier comparison (COG-023) once margin is confirmed healthy.

test.method: Check margin against threshold before every first bulk order on a SKU.
test.measure: Contribution margin at time of bulk order decision
test.read_point: Before the PO is drafted

title: Check the factory-direct versus intermediary price gap as a negotiation sanity check
hypothesis: If we compute the gap between an intermediary's price and the factory-direct landed cost, then we know how much markup an intermediary carries, because a hidden markup only becomes visible once both numbers sit side by side.

signal.check: A distributor or trading company is the current source for a SKU and no factory-direct comparison has been run.

expected_effect.size: one swag example showed about 30% below the domestic price

risk.note: A comparison only; no supplier change required to run it.

prerequisites: A factory-direct quote (COG-021)
The current intermediary price
steps: Take the current intermediary unit price for the SKU.
Take the factory-direct landed cost per unit for the same spec and quantity.
Compute the percentage gap between the two.
Use the gap as a data point in the next negotiation or sourcing decision, not as a final number on its own.

test.method: Recompute the gap whenever a new factory-direct quote comes in.
test.measure: Percentage gap between intermediary price and factory-direct landed cost
test.read_point: Whenever a new factory-direct quote is received

title: Never shoot creative, set a price or commit a launch date before a sample from the exact factory
hypothesis: If creative, pricing and launch dates wait for a physical sample from the exact factory making the SKU, then the store avoids shooting or pricing against a product that will not match what ships, because a factory's word on quality is not enough.

signal.check: A photo shoot, pre-order page or launch date is booked on a sample from a different factory, or the same factory's other product.

risk.note: Skipping this and shooting on the wrong sample can mean reshooting creative and delaying a launch.

prerequisites: A sample ordered from this exact factory for this exact product
steps: Confirm the sample in hand came from the exact factory and product line being launched, not a sister factory.
Hold any shoot, price commitment or launch date until that sample is inspected.
Compare the sample against the approved reference (COG-030) before approving it for creative use.

test.method: Check the sample log for a match between the sample source and the launch factory before every shoot.
test.measure: Share of shoots or launch dates with a same-factory sample confirmed first
test.read_point: Before every new product shoot or launch date

title: Run the 3-stage sample gate with a hard stop at the production sample
hypothesis: If every new supplier and SKU goes through strike-off, pre-production and a production sample that must match before bulk, then a mismatch is caught before it reaches a customer, because a production sample that slips this gate becomes a return and a bad review.

signal.check: A bulk PO is planned with no signed-off production sample matching the pre-production standard.

risk.note: Adds time before bulk; the risk of skipping it is a bulk-order defect.

prerequisites: A tech pack version (COG-003)
An approved reference sample
steps: Stage 1, strike-off: approve materials, colours and prints against Pantone and material specs.
Stage 2, pre-production: check the sample matches the tech pack exactly; for apparel, check size grading across multiple samples.
Stage 3, production sample: built immediately before mass production, compared against the approved pre-production sample.
If the production sample does not match, stop. Do not proceed to bulk.
Log each stage's sign-off with a date and the version it was checked against.

test.method: Check the sample log shows every stage signed off before the PO is released.
test.measure: Share of POs with all 3 sample stages signed off
test.read_point: Before releasing the balance payment on any bulk PO

title: Score supplier communication and reliability during the sample stage
hypothesis: If we score how well a candidate follows instructions and sends unprompted updates during the sample stage, then the final supplier pick weighs reliability, not only sample quality, because the supplier who warns first also warns before a promo-week delay.

signal.check: Multiple candidates are in the sample stage, but only sample quality is being scored, not communication.

risk.note: A scoring habit, no direct cost.

prerequisites: At least 2 candidates in the sample stage
steps: Track whether each candidate followed instructions exactly on the sample request.
Track whether they sent status updates without being asked.
Record a communication score next to the sample quality score.
Weigh both scores when choosing the final supplier.

test.method: Compare communication scores against sample quality scores when the final pick is made.
test.measure: Communication score per candidate at final decision
test.read_point: At final supplier selection

title: Keep one approved sample in-house and one at the factory as a reference
hypothesis: If one approved sample stays in-house and one stays at the factory, then every future QC check, PDP shoot and returns dispute has a physical reference to judge against, because a judgment with no physical reference is only a guess.

signal.check: No approved sample is on hand at the brand's own location after pre-production sign-off.

risk.note: A logistics step, shipping one physical unit.

prerequisites: A pre-production sample approved
steps: On approval, keep one sample copy at the brand's own location.
Leave one copy at the factory as its reference.
Log both copies' location and an owner responsible for each.
Use the in-house copy for every future QC, PDP or dispute comparison.

test.method: Check both reference copies exist and their locations are logged.
test.measure: Whether both copies are logged with a location and owner
test.read_point: After pre-production approval

title: Compare each candidate's sample side by side against the approved reference
hypothesis: If a factory's sample is compared directly against the approved reference sample on the attributes customers mention most in reviews, then deviations that matter to customers get caught early, because a general quality impression can miss the specific things buyers notice.

signal.check: A sample is judged as good or bad overall, with no side-by-side comparison against the reference on specific attributes.

risk.note: A comparison step.

prerequisites: An approved reference sample (COG-031)
Top review-mentioned attributes for the product
steps: List the attributes customers mention most in reviews and returns.
Put the reference sample and the candidate's sample side by side.
Score each attribute and record any deviation, even a small one.
Repeat at every sample stage, not only the final one.

test.method: Track the number of deviations recorded per stage across suppliers.
test.measure: Deviation count per sample stage
test.read_point: At every sample stage

title: Never treat a passed sample as a guarantee of bulk quality
hypothesis: If the team keeps the production sample gate and pre-shipment QC active even after a sample passes, then a bulk batch with defects the sample did not show still gets caught, because a good sample is not a guarantee, and 2 real bulk orders had defects after a passed sample.

signal.check: A passed sample is tempting the team to skip the production sample gate or pre-shipment QC on the bulk order.

risk.note: Skipping the gate after a passed sample is exactly the mistake this idea prevents.

steps: Keep the production sample gate (COG-029) on the critical path for every bulk PO, regardless of an earlier passed sample.
Keep pre-shipment QC (COG-062) booked regardless of sample results.
Brief the team that a passed sample is not a bulk guarantee, so neither gate gets skipped under launch pressure.

test.method: Check that both gates ran even when the sample passed cleanly.
test.measure: Share of bulk POs where both gates ran regardless of sample result
test.read_point: On every bulk PO

title: Test a cheaper competing supplier with a small, fully inspected batch first
hypothesis: If a cheaper competing supplier gets a small test order that is fully inspected before any volume moves, then a bad switch shows up as a test-batch defect rate, not as customer returns, because a failed switch shows up in returns and ratings before it shows up as a saving.

signal.check: A competing supplier quotes materially lower than the incumbent, and a move is being considered without a test batch.

expected_effect.size: one case tested 500 units against a 20% cheaper quote and found most defective, so the incumbent was kept

risk.note: The test order cost is the acceptable loss if the new supplier fails; the incumbent stays active in the meantime.

prerequisites: The new supplier passed shortlisting and sample stages
The incumbent's own observed defect rate on file
steps: Keep the incumbent's order unchanged.
Place a small test order with the new supplier at an acceptable loss size.
Inspect the entire test batch, not a sample of it.
Compare the test batch's defect rate against the incumbent's observed rate.
Move volume only if the new rate is comparable; otherwise keep the incumbent.

test.method: Compare measured defect rates between the test batch and the incumbent's history.
test.measure: Defect rate, test batch versus incumbent
test.read_point: After the full test batch is inspected

title: Vet a real alternate factory before any cost-down negotiation
hypothesis: If a genuinely vetted alternate factory is in hand before a cost-down call, then the negotiation has real leverage, because leverage entered late in a conversation is hard to build in the moment.

signal.check: A cost-down or terms negotiation is coming up with no independently vetted alternate factory in hand.

risk.note: Vetting cost only if not already part of the standing backup process.

prerequisites: A backup factory candidate (COG-017)
steps: Confirm a backup factory has been independently vetted with a quote and, ideally, a passed sample.
Prepare its quote on identical terms to the incumbent's for direct comparison.
Bring this into the negotiation brief before the cost-down call.
Be ready to actually switch if the incumbent will not move and the backup is real.

test.method: Check the negotiation brief lists a real, current backup quote before the call.
test.measure: Whether a vetted backup exists at the time of negotiation
test.read_point: Before every cost-down call

title: Buy and reverse-engineer competitor products before a cost-down negotiation
hypothesis: If competitor products are bought and reverse-engineered for materials and construction before a cost-down call, then the negotiation is grounded in what similar products actually cost to make, because a category cost picture built beforehand is stronger than one improvised in the room.

signal.check: A negotiation is coming up with no competitor teardown findings prepared.

risk.note: Cost of buying competitor products; never copy their text, logos or design in the brand's own product.

steps: Buy competitor products in the same category.
Take them apart and estimate materials, construction and likely cost.
Record findings as evidence for the negotiation, not as a design source.
Bring findings into the negotiation brief alongside the backup quote (COG-035).

test.method: Check the negotiation brief includes competitor teardown findings.
test.measure: Whether teardown findings are documented before the call
test.read_point: Before every cost-down call

title: Learn the category's normal factory margin before negotiating
hypothesis: If the category's typical factory margin is learned from people who ran procurement at similar-scale brands before a negotiation, then the ask is grounded in a realistic target, because negotiating with no benchmark risks asking for either too little or an unrealistic cut.

signal.check: A cost-down negotiation is planned with no idea what a normal factory margin looks like in this category.

expected_effect.size: unknown, category margin bands vary; one jewelry example cited about 5 to 9% factory EBITDA margin, not for reuse in other categories

risk.note: A research step.

steps: Identify people who have run procurement at brands of a similar scale in this category.
Ask about typical factory margin bands for this product type.
Record the source and the category, since margin bands do not transfer across categories.
Use it as a reference point in the negotiation, not a guaranteed number.

test.method: Check whether a category benchmark is on record before the negotiation.
test.measure: Whether a benchmark and its source are documented
test.read_point: Before every cost-down call

title: Choose a negotiation posture based on whether the supplier relationship is strategic or replaceable
hypothesis: If the owner decides upfront whether to use a competing-quote posture or a growth-partnership posture, then the negotiation matches the relationship, because a transactional supplier responds to competition while a strategic one responds to a shared growth story.

signal.check: A cost-down negotiation is about to start with no decision on posture, partnership framing or competing-quote framing.

risk.note: Overplaying a competing-quote posture with a sole-source supplier risks the relationship.

prerequisites: A vetted backup (COG-035) if going with competing-quote framing
steps: Decide with the owner whether the supplier is strategic, one the brand wants for years, or transactional.
For a strategic supplier, use partnership framing (COG-039).
For a transactional or complacent supplier with a real backup, use competing-quote framing.
Never bluff a competing quote without a real backup in hand.

test.method: Record the chosen posture and the outcome of the negotiation.
test.measure: Cost or terms movement by posture chosen
test.read_point: After each negotiation closes

title: Frame a cost-down as a growth partnership, in units, not price talk
hypothesis: If a cost-down for a strategic supplier is framed as shared growth, with the ownership or growth story named, the P&L shared only as percentages, and volume expressed in units by year, then the factory responds to a real growth plan instead of a price demand, because factories respond to units, not marketing language.

signal.check: A negotiation with a supplier the brand wants to keep for years is being framed only as a price ask, with no growth story or unit plan.

risk.note: A framing choice for a conversation.

prerequisites: A real growth or demand plan in units
The posture decision (COG-038) set to partnership
steps: Convert the demand plan into a units-by-year figure the factory can act on.
Name the change driving the ask, such as new ownership or a planned growth push.
Share the P&L only as rounded percentages, not exact dollar figures.
Offer to share one specific cost, such as financing, to make the ask two-sided.

test.method: Compare the units quoted to the factory against the actual demand plan on file.
test.measure: Match between quoted units and the demand plan
test.read_point: At the negotiation and again at the next demand plan update

title: Write every price-break threshold and credit into the supplier agreement
hypothesis: If volume price breaks are written as forward credits tied to a specific threshold, not a verbal promise, then the credit actually shows up on invoices, because a verbal price break with no written trigger has no way to be enforced.

signal.check: A supplier has offered a better price at volume with no written threshold or credit rate recorded.

expected_effect.size: one jewelry example cited about $2 to $3 per unit of credit at higher utilisation on a $42 labor line

risk.note: A documentation step.

prerequisites: A BOM with volume-sensitive lines (COG-004)
steps: Ask, per BOM line, how much idle machine time or labor capacity the supplier has, and what volume would lower that cost.
Agree a specific threshold in units and a credit per unit above that threshold.
Write the threshold and credit into the supplier agreement as a forward-only credit, not retroactive.
Set up invoice reconciliation against this threshold (COG-041).

test.method: Check every agreed break has a written threshold and credit rate on file.
test.measure: Share of price breaks with a written threshold
test.read_point: Immediately after each negotiation

title: Reconcile every invoice against the agreed price-break credits
hypothesis: If every invoice past a price-break threshold is checked against the expected credit, then a missed credit is caught and chased, because a credit agreed verbally or on paper does not appear automatically on an invoice.

signal.check: A price-break threshold has been agreed but no one checks invoices against it after the threshold is crossed.

expected_effect.size: unknown, equal to the variance recovered per invoice

risk.note: An ongoing check, not a one-time task.

prerequisites: A written price-break threshold and credit (COG-040)
steps: Compute the expected invoice using base price minus any credit due for units past the threshold.
Compare the expected invoice against the actual invoice for each period.
Flag any variance and send it to the ops lead to chase with the supplier.
Track the invoice reconciliation as a recurring monthly task, not a one-time check.

test.method: Run the reconciliation on every invoice after a threshold is crossed.
test.measure: Variance between expected and actual invoice amount
test.read_point: On every invoice past an agreed threshold

title: Ask the factory to pass through its own sub-vendor volume breaks
hypothesis: If we ask whether the factory's own sub-vendors give it volume breaks and negotiate for that saving to pass through, then cost reductions the factory already gets are shared with the brand, because that saving otherwise stays inside the factory's margin.

signal.check: A BOM line is a bought-in component with no question asked about the factory's own sub-vendor volume terms.

expected_effect.size: one garment example cited about $1 off per zipper at higher factory volume

risk.note: A question to ask during a BOM review.

prerequisites: A BOM with a mapped sub-vendor layer (COG-004)
steps: Identify every bought-in component in the BOM.
Ask the factory whether its own supplier for that component gives volume breaks.
Negotiate for a share of that break to pass through to the brand.
Record any agreed pass-through as its own credit line in the invoice reconciliation (COG-041).

test.method: Check whether any pass-through credit appears on invoices after the ask.
test.measure: Pass-through credit amount recorded per component
test.read_point: At the next BOM review or negotiation

title: Review the BOM with the supplier yearly and ask what unlocks the next price break
hypothesis: If the BOM is reviewed with the supplier at least once a year, line by line, asking what volume unlocks the next break, then cost reductions are found on a schedule instead of by accident, because a mature product with no cost review in years likely has room.

signal.check: A supplier relationship is over a year old with no dated BOM review on file.

risk.note: A recurring review, no direct cost.

prerequisites: A BOM (COG-004)
steps: Diary a yearly BOM review with each core supplier.
Go through the BOM line by line and ask what volume unlocks the next break.
Ask when COGS last declined on this SKU (COG-011).
Record the next threshold per line for tracking.

test.method: Check whether a dated yearly review exists for every supplier relationship over a year old.
test.measure: Share of suppliers with a review in the last 12 months
test.read_point: Once a year, per supplier

title: Pay a bit more for order-resize flexibility in a new SKU's first runs
hypothesis: If the first 1 to 2 production runs of a new SKU accept a slightly higher unit cost in exchange for the right to resize or pivot the order, then the store avoids trapping cash in unsold stock, because sell-through is unknown until paid traffic actually runs against the PDP.
does_not_apply_when: The SKU already has proven sell-through and margin (COG-026).

signal.check: A new SKU with no sell-through history is about to place its first production run at the lowest available unit price.

expected_effect.size: one cautionary case: founders who saved about $2 per unit ended with warehouses of unsold stock

risk.note: Slightly higher unit cost in exchange for flexibility; the alternative risk is unsold stock.

steps: Identify the SKU as new with no sell-through history.
Ask the factory for a written resize or pivot window on the first PO, even at a slightly higher unit cost.
Use the first 1 to 2 runs to learn sell-through, quality consistency and delay points.
Negotiate a deeper volume discount only once real sell-through data exists.

test.method: Track sell-through and stock levels through the first 2 production runs before negotiating a volume discount.
test.measure: Days of stock and sell-through rate through the first 2 runs
test.read_point: After the first and second production runs

title: Stop a cost-down before it triggers supplier retaliation
hypothesis: If a cost-down negotiation stops before the point where the supplier would recover the cut through cheaper materials, skipped QC or slower timelines, then the saving does not come back as a defect rate increase or a missed promo, because that is exactly how a squeezed supplier recovers margin.

signal.check: A cost-down has been pushed hard on a supplier the brand plans to keep, with no check on defect rate or on-time delivery afterward.

risk.note: A monitoring discipline paired with the negotiation.

prerequisites: Baseline defect rate and on-time delivery history for the supplier
steps: Record the supplier's defect rate and on-time delivery before any cost-down.
After the cost-down, compare the same metrics on the next few shipments.
If defect rate rises or timelines slip, treat it as retaliation and ease off the push.
For a relationship kept long-term, offer the top of any known margin band while conditions are good, expecting reciprocity in a shock.

test.method: Compare defect rate and on-time delivery before and after each cost-down.
test.measure: Defect rate and on-time ship rate, before versus after
test.read_point: On the next 2 to 3 shipments after a cost-down

title: Monitor commodity-priced BOM inputs on a set cadence with multiple quotes
hypothesis: If a BOM line with a market-priced input, like gold, diamonds or chipsets, is checked against spot price on a set cadence with quotes from several sub-vendors, then the supplier's markup on spot stays visible, because it otherwise stays hidden inside a single supplier's quote.
does_not_apply_when: No BOM line has a public or fast-moving market price.

signal.check: A BOM line has a market-priced input and the PDP price has not moved even though spot price has.

risk.note: A monitoring task.

prerequisites: A BOM line identified as commodity-priced
steps: Identify every BOM line tied to a public or fast-moving market price.
Set a re-quote cadence, monthly is one operator's practice, from multiple sub-vendors.
Record spot price and quoted price side by side for each pull.
Flag any widening gap for the next negotiation.

test.method: Track the gap between spot price and quoted price over time.
test.measure: Spot-to-quote gap per commodity input
test.read_point: On the set cadence, at least monthly for active commodity lines

title: Benchmark component costs at category trade fairs
hypothesis: If the team attends category trade fairs about twice a year, then it gets an independent read on component pricing outside any single supplier's quote, because a supplier's own quote alone gives no outside comparison.

signal.check: No component pricing benchmark has been checked outside the current supplier's own quotes in the last 6 months.

risk.note: Travel and time cost; low risk otherwise.

steps: Identify the relevant trade fair for the product category.
Attend about twice a year and collect component pricing from multiple exhibitors.
Record findings alongside the BOM's current supplier prices.
Use gaps as evidence in the next negotiation.

test.method: Compare trade fair pricing intelligence against current supplier quotes.
test.measure: Gap between trade fair pricing and current quoted cost
test.read_point: After each trade fair visit

title: Consider buying a concentrated raw material directly at volume
hypothesis: If the brand buys a large-COGS-share raw material directly and supplies it to the factory as an assembler, then supplier markup on that input is removed, because the trade-off is taking on the commodity's price risk directly instead of paying the supplier to carry it.
does_not_apply_when: The component's COGS share is small, or the brand cannot absorb a spot price swing.

signal.check: A component has a large share of COGS (F11) and trades on a public market, with no direct-purchase option considered.

risk.note: The brand takes on commodity price risk directly, and a spot move then hits margin without the supplier absorbing it first.

prerequisites: A BOM with concentration shares computed (COG-089)
steps: Identify a component with a large COGS share and a public spot price.
Assess the brand's ability to absorb a spot price swing.
Get the owner's written sign-off on taking on commodity price risk directly.
Arrange to buy the raw material and supply it to the factory as an assembler.

test.method: Track landed cost and margin before and after the direct-purchase switch, alongside the spot price over the same period.
test.measure: Landed cost per unit and margin, before versus after
test.read_point: After the first shipment made from directly supplied material

title: Offer to share a specific cost with the supplier to make a negotiation two-sided
hypothesis: If the brand offers to share one specific cost, such as financing, with a strategic supplier, then the cost-down conversation reads as two-sided instead of one-sided, because a purely one-way ask is harder for a supplier to agree to.

signal.check: A partnership-framed negotiation is planned with no specific shared cost being offered.

risk.note: A framing offer within a negotiation.

prerequisites: The partnership negotiation framing (COG-039)
steps: Identify a specific cost the brand could offer to share, such as financing cost.
Bring a proposed split into the negotiation as a concrete number, not a vague offer.
Present it alongside the growth-in-units story.
Record the agreed split if the supplier accepts.

test.method: Track whether offering a shared cost changes the outcome versus negotiations without one.
test.measure: Price or terms movement with versus without a shared-cost offer
test.read_point: After the negotiation closes

title: Treat payment terms as float and push for longer terms as trust grows
hypothesis: If payment terms are evaluated as float, terms days minus production lead time minus a buffer, and pushed longer as track record grows, then cash is freed for ads and the next reorder, because a supplier's paper terms and the actual cash mechanism can differ.

signal.check: The next PO's deposit is competing with the ad budget for the same weeks, and float has not been computed for the current terms.

expected_effect.size: one example: 90-day terms minus 30-day lead time gave 60 days of float before buffer

risk.note: A calculation and negotiation ask.

prerequisites: Current payment terms and production lead time per supplier
steps: Map the real dates: deposit, production start, ship, land, sellable, payout.
Compute float as payment terms days minus production lead time days minus a buffer for ordering mistakes (F1).
For a new supplier, negotiate whatever terms fit the brand's own cash needs.
For an established supplier, ask for longer terms as volume and trust build over time.

test.method: Track float days per supplier over time as terms are renegotiated.
test.measure: Float days per supplier
test.read_point: At every terms renegotiation

title: Default to Trade Assurance for a new or unproven supplier
hypothesis: If every new or unproven supplier is paid through the platform's protected order route with spec, chat and payment on-platform, then the deposit is protected, because that deposit is cash the store also needs for ads and the next reorder.

signal.check: A new or unproven supplier is set to be paid by direct transfer with no protected route or owner sign-off.

risk.note: A payment routing decision.

steps: Check whether the supplier has a history of compliant bulk delivery to the brand.
If not, keep the spec, chat and payment on the platform's protected order route.
Record the payment route chosen on the PO.
Never pay off-platform to a new supplier to speed a shipment.

test.method: Check the payment route recorded on every PO to a new or unproven supplier.
test.measure: Share of new-supplier POs using the protected route
test.read_point: On every new supplier's first PO

title: Allow direct transfer only for a proven supplier, with owner sign-off, for a real discount
hypothesis: If direct transfer is used only for a supplier that has already delivered compliant bulk, and only with the owner's sign-off for a real platform-fee discount, then the store keeps the cost saving without giving up protection on an unproven relationship.
does_not_apply_when: The supplier has no track record of compliant bulk delivery, or there is no owner sign-off.

signal.check: A proven supplier offers a discount for paying by direct transfer instead of the protected route.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the discount is the platform fee avoided

risk.note: Direct transfer removes the platform's dispute protection, so it should only be used with a proven, trusted supplier.

prerequisites: A documented history of compliant bulk delivery from this supplier
steps: Confirm the supplier has already delivered compliant bulk to the brand.
Confirm the discount offered is worth the loss of platform protection.
Get the owner's explicit sign-off before switching to direct transfer.
Record the choice and the reason on the PO.

test.method: Track whether any dispute arises after switching a supplier to direct transfer.
test.measure: Dispute count and discount amount realised
test.read_point: After each shipment paid by direct transfer

title: Tie the balance payment to a passed pre-shipment QC report
hypothesis: If the balance payment clause names the QC report as the release condition instead of the ship date, then the brand does not pay for a shipment before knowing it passed inspection, because paying on the ship date removes the leverage to fix a problem before departure.

signal.check: A PO's payment clause ties the balance to the ship date, not a passed inspection report.

risk.note: A contract clause change.

prerequisites: A pre-shipment inspection booked (COG-061)
steps: Write the payment clause so the balance releases only after a passed QC report, not on the ship date.
Agree the deposit and balance split with the supplier, commonly a 30/70 split in practice.
Confirm the clause is in the signed PO before production starts.

test.method: Check the balance release date against the QC pass date on every shipment.
test.measure: Share of shipments where balance was released only after a pass
test.read_point: On every production shipment

title: Ask about consignment where the product has resale or reclaim value
hypothesis: If the brand asks an established supplier about consignment, paying only when units sell, in a category with resale or reclaim value, then cash stays free until the product actually sells, because consignment is the strongest form of supplier financing where it is available.
does_not_apply_when: No reclaim or resale value, a new relationship, or a geography where the supplier cannot take back unsold stock.

signal.check: The category has residual or resale value and the supplier relationship has a clean payment and dispute record, but consignment has never been discussed.

risk.note: An ask, not a commitment; not generally available to a new or small brand.

prerequisites: An established supplier relationship with a clean payment history
steps: Confirm the product has real resale or reclaim value to the supplier.
Confirm the fulfilment geography lets the supplier take back unsold stock.
Write down both conditions before making the ask.
Raise consignment with the supplier as an established-relationship request, not a new-brand ask.

test.method: Track whether the supplier agrees, and the cash freed if so.
test.measure: Cash conversion days before versus after any agreed consignment terms
test.read_point: After the ask is made and, if accepted, on the next order

title: Ask for a hybrid payment cadence with a buffer for the brand's own ordering mistakes
hypothesis: If consignment is refused but the brand asks for standard net terms plus a smaller regular cadence such as weekly, with no penalty for its own over-ordering mistakes, then float still improves without needing full consignment, because a wrong size or colour mix is a mistake the buffer should cover.

signal.check: Full consignment (COG-054) was refused, but the store's own payouts already arrive on a weekly cadence.

risk.note: A terms ask.

prerequisites: An established relationship
Consignment declined or unavailable
steps: Ask for standard net terms on the invoice.
Propose a smaller, regular payment cadence that matches the store's own payout cycle.
Ask for no penalty on the brand's own over-ordering mistakes.
Add a float buffer to F1 for those mistakes once the cadence is agreed.

test.method: Track float days and cadence adherence after the hybrid terms start.
test.measure: Float days with the hybrid cadence
test.read_point: After the first full cadence cycle

title: Ask if the supplier uses export credit insurance to extend terms
hypothesis: If we ask whether the supplier uses export credit insurance to extend terms, then the brand knows whether it will be credit-graded on its own books and payment history, because a credit grade depends on management accounts, payment history and past disputes.

signal.check: The supplier's country has a developed credit-insurance ecosystem, and the relationship is established, but this has never been asked.

risk.note: A diligence question.

prerequisites: A supplier in a country with export credit insurance available
Clean books, payment history and no open disputes
steps: Ask the supplier whether it uses export credit insurance to extend terms.
Ask what audit firm grades the relationship and what it checks.
Review the brand's own books, payment history and any open disputes before an audit happens.
Resolve or disclose any old dispute before the terms request.

test.method: Track whether the ask leads to a credit grade and extended terms.
test.measure: Terms extended and grade received
test.read_point: After the ask and any resulting audit

title: Ask if the supplier uses invoice factoring to extend terms
hypothesis: If we ask whether the supplier uses invoice factoring to extend terms, then the brand can weigh that against its own working-capital options, because factoring is a different mechanism from credit insurance and changes what the supplier can offer.

signal.check: The relationship is established and terms are being negotiated, but factoring has never come up as an option.

risk.note: A diligence question.

prerequisites: An established supplier relationship
steps: Ask the supplier whether it uses invoice factoring to extend terms.
Ask what advance rate and bank or lender the factoring uses.
Compare the resulting terms option against the brand's own financing choices.
Record findings for the terms proposal.

test.method: Track whether factoring-backed terms are offered after the ask.
test.measure: Terms offered with versus without factoring in play
test.read_point: After the ask is made

title: Make financing cost an explicit BOM line and negotiate the split
hypothesis: If supplier financing cost is written as its own BOM line and expressed as currency per unit, percent of COGS and percent of revenue, then the brand can compare it honestly against other lenders, because a financing rate hidden inside the unit price can look cheaper than it is.

signal.check: Extended payment terms exist with a financing charge buried in the unit price, not shown as its own line.

expected_effect.size: one example: about 5 to 6% of financed COGS per year, about $6 per unit at 100,000 units; a US inventory lender warning of 30 to 40% effective versus a 10% headline rate

risk.note: A transparency and comparison step.

prerequisites: Terms that include supplier financing
steps: Ask the supplier to state financing cost as its own line, separate from unit price.
Compute financing cost per unit, as percent of COGS, and as percent of revenue.
Compare against other working-capital options before calling it cheap.
Negotiate a specific split of the financing cost between brand and factory.

test.method: Compare the 3 financing cost figures against the brand's other lending options.
test.measure: Financing cost as percent of revenue versus alternative lenders
test.read_point: Before agreeing to any supplier-financed terms

title: Structure a partner-financed bulk buy for a cash-capped recurring SKU
hypothesis: If a recurring SKU's deepest volume tier is funded by a partner who adds capital while the brand pays its usual unit price only as units are consumed, then the brand reaches a better volume tier without locking its own cash, because the ceiling on the deepest tier is cash, not demand.
does_not_apply_when: No recurring reorder pattern exists, or no trusted partner with capital is available.

signal.check: A SKU reorders several times a year and the deepest volume tier would lock more cash than the brand can spare.

expected_effect.size: one commenter's client example paid about $10 per unit landed, consuming units as sold

risk.note: Needs written ownership and repayment terms; no legal or accounting detail in the source.

prerequisites: A recurring reorder SKU
A trusted partner with capital
Legal review available
steps: Confirm the SKU reorders several times a year and the deepest tier's cash lock exceeds what the brand can spare.
Find a partner willing to add capital to reach the full volume tier.
Draft terms: stock ownership, repayment schedule, and what happens to unsold units.
Compute float (F1) and financing cost (F10) under the proposed structure.
Send the draft to the owner and a lawyer before anything moves.

test.method: Track cash freed and cost per unit under the partner-financed structure versus a self-funded order.
test.measure: Cash locked and landed cost per unit, partner-financed versus self-funded
test.read_point: After the first partner-financed order

title: Hand float days, cash locked and financing cost to finance at each close
hypothesis: If sourcing sends float days, cash locked in POs and financing cost to finance at every monthly close, then working-capital decisions are made with current sourcing inputs, because distribution versus reinvestment decisions depend on numbers only sourcing has.

signal.check: The monthly close happens with no current float, cash-locked or financing-cost figures handed from sourcing.

risk.note: A reporting handoff, no decision made by sourcing itself.

prerequisites: Float days computed per supplier (COG-050)
Cash-locked figures from open POs
steps: Compute current float days per supplier.
Total cash locked across all open purchase orders.
Total any active financing cost.
Send all 3, with their dates, to finance before the monthly close.

test.method: Check whether finance receives all 3 figures at each close.
test.measure: Share of closes with all 3 inputs delivered on time
test.read_point: At every monthly close

title: Book a mandatory third-party pre-shipment inspection before the container leaves
hypothesis: If every production shipment gets a third-party inspection booked before loading, with the balance released only on a pass, then a defect is caught and fixed by the factory before it becomes a customer refund, because once goods are on the water they cannot be fixed.

signal.check: A production shipment is scheduled to leave with no third-party inspection booked.

expected_effect.size: the inspection cost is about $200 against problems that can run into thousands per shipment

risk.note: About $200 per inspection; the risk is skipping it, not doing it.

prerequisites: An inspection provider and rate
The spec version and approved sample photos
steps: Book the third-party inspection for the date before container loading.
Send the inspector the spec version, acceptance attributes and photos of the approved sample.
Scope: random units tested, measurements, packaging and labelling, carton weight, photographs of everything.
Read the report and compare the sampled defect rate against the buffer rate (F7).
On a pass, release the balance. On a fail, the factory fixes before departure and is re-inspected.

test.method: Check that a passed report exists before every balance release.
test.measure: Share of shipments with a report on file before balance release
test.read_point: Before every production shipment leaves

title: Size the order's defect buffer from the observed defect rate
hypothesis: If the extra units ordered to cover defects are sized from the supplier's own observed defect rate instead of a fixed surplus, then the order quantity matches real risk, because a fixed surplus either wastes cash or leaves the brand short.

signal.check: A bulk order is being sized with a flat extra percentage with no reference to this supplier's inspection history.

expected_effect.size: one case ordered 10% extra and saw about 3% defective (300 of 10,000)

risk.note: A sizing calculation.

prerequisites: Inspection history for the supplier, or an owner-set floor rate if none exists
steps: Compute the observed defect rate from the supplier's last inspected shipments.
Take the higher of the observed rate and the owner's floor rate for a supplier with no history.
Compute order quantity as demand units divided by 1 minus the buffer rate (F7).
Tighten the buffer rate after each new inspected shipment.

test.method: Compare the buffer rate used against the actual defect rate found at inspection.
test.measure: Buffer rate versus actual defect rate
test.read_point: After each inspected shipment

title: Decide and record whether to return or absorb defective units
hypothesis: If every shipment with defects above the buffer gets a recorded return-or-absorb decision and its effective landed cost, then the true margin impact of absorbing a defect is visible, because an absorbed defect raises the cost per sellable unit.

signal.check: A shipment came back with defects above the buffer rate and no decision has been recorded on return versus absorb.

risk.note: A decision and recording step.

prerequisites: A completed inspection or receiving count with defect data
steps: Compare the shipment's defect count against the buffer rate.
Decide case by case whether returning the defective units is worth the time versus absorbing the loss.
Record the decision and the effective landed cost per sellable unit (F6).
Re-run the margin gate (COG-026) on the SKU with the new effective cost.

test.method: Track the recorded decision and resulting effective cost per shipment.
test.measure: Effective landed cost per unit after an absorbed defect
test.read_point: After every inspection that finds defects above the buffer

title: Run a written QC checklist before every production run ships
hypothesis: If every production run goes through a written checklist before it ships, then fewer steps get skipped under launch pressure, because an unwritten process depends on someone remembering every step every time.

signal.check: A production run is about to ship with no written checklist ticked off against it.

risk.note: A documentation habit.

prerequisites: A written checklist covering spec, sample and QC steps
steps: Build a checklist covering the exact spec, sample approval and QC steps relevant to this SKU.
Tick every item with a date before the ship date.
Store the completed checklist with the shipment's records.
Review checklists periodically for steps that are consistently skipped.

test.method: Check the checklist is complete before every shipment leaves.
test.measure: Share of shipments with a fully ticked checklist before departure
test.read_point: Before every shipment

title: Split customer returns into supplier-fault and fit or expectation buckets
hypothesis: If every customer return is tagged as either a supplier fault or a fit or expectation problem, then a real supplier-fault return feeds the observed defect rate and the next negotiation, because damaged and not-as-described returns are a different signal than a size or fit issue.

signal.check: Return reasons show damaged or not as described on a SKU, with no split between supplier-fault and fit or expectation reasons.

expected_effect.size: unknown, this is a measurement improvement, feeding a more accurate observed rate

risk.note: A tagging change to the returns process.

prerequisites: A customer returns flow with recorded reasons
steps: Add a supplier-fault versus fit-or-expectation tag to every return reason.
Route fit or expectation returns to the PDP and size chart review.
Route supplier-fault returns into the observed defect rate (F7) and the next negotiation (COG-045).
Report both buckets separately per SKU per month.

test.method: Track the split and whether supplier-fault returns move the observed defect rate.
test.measure: Return count per bucket per SKU per month
test.read_point: Monthly returns review

title: Reconcile receiving counts and defects against the inspection report on arrival
hypothesis: If the receiving count and defect count on arrival are checked against the pre-shipment inspection report, then a gap between what was inspected and what arrived is caught and raised with the inspector, keeping the observed defect rate accurate.

signal.check: A shipment has arrived with no comparison run between the receiving count and the inspection report.

expected_effect.size: unknown, this improves measurement accuracy of the observed rate

risk.note: A reconciliation check.

prerequisites: A pre-shipment inspection report (COG-061)
steps: On arrival, count units received and defects found.
Compare against the pre-shipment inspection report's figures.
Raise any gap with the inspector.
Update the supplier's observed defect rate with the reconciled figure.

test.method: Check that a reconciliation record exists for every arrived shipment.
test.measure: Share of shipments with a reconciliation on file
test.read_point: On every shipment's arrival

title: Choose freight mode by weight, volume and the launch calendar
hypothesis: If freight mode is picked by weight, volume and the date already fixed on the marketing calendar, then the store avoids forced, expensive air freight, because a late order turns into forced air cargo exactly when a launch's margin needs protecting.

signal.check: A launch or promo date is fixed and the freight mode has not yet been chosen against it.

expected_effect.size: one rush case: an air cargo quote of about $2,000 for a small shipment near Q4, rejected in favour of sea

risk.note: A planning decision.

prerequisites: Product weight and volume
The launch or promo date
Forwarder quotes for air and sea
steps: Compute the shipment's weight, volume and required land date.
Use air for small, light or urgent batches; sea for heavy or bulky restocks; premium courier for large orders with a good relationship; small-parcel post only for dropship-scale batches.
Get quotes with transit days for the relevant modes.
Choose the mode that lands on time at the lowest freight cost per unit.

test.method: Compare freight cost per unit and land date across the modes considered.
test.measure: Freight cost per unit for the chosen mode versus the fastest mode
test.read_point: Before booking the shipment

title: Hybridize freight: air a small first batch, then sea-restock
hypothesis: If a small first batch flies in by air so the PDP can go live on time, while the bulk of the order comes by sea, then the launch date holds without paying full air freight on the whole order, because most brands in the source hybridise for exactly this reason.

signal.check: A new SKU's launch date is close and the full sea shipment will not land in time.

risk.note: Air freight on the small batch costs more per unit, offset by holding the launch date.

prerequisites: A launch date already set
Both an air and a sea quote
steps: Compute the sea shipment's expected land date against the launch date.
If sea will not land in time, split the order: a small batch by air, the rest by sea.
Time the air batch to land just before the launch date.
Let the sea batch restock once the launch batch starts selling.

test.method: Track whether the PDP went live on the launch date and how quickly the sea restock arrived.
test.measure: Days between launch date and actual PDP live date
test.read_point: At launch and at the sea restock's arrival

title: Start planning the next shipment the day the current one lands
hypothesis: If the next shipment's planning starts the day the current one lands, not when stock runs low, then stock stays in place for promotions already on the calendar, because total lead time makes the trigger the landing date, not the stock level.

signal.check: The next shipment's planning has not started even though the current one has already landed.

risk.note: A scheduling discipline.

prerequisites: Measured total lead time from the last 3 shipments (F2)
