steps: Compute total lead time from order release to sellable stock, from measured history (F2).
Diary the next shipment's planning start for the day the current one lands.
Use the forwarder's actual quote and the brand's own shipment history over generic planning defaults.
Confirm the PO date that keeps land date ahead of any promo or launch.

test.method: Check whether the next PO's planning started on the day the current shipment landed.
test.measure: Days between landing and next-PO planning start
test.read_point: On every shipment landing

title: Order heavy or bulky items early enough for sea freight
hypothesis: If heavy or bulky items are ordered ahead of the season, inside the sea transit window, then air freight is not forced later, because a late order on a heavy item makes air cargo or a missed season the only options.

signal.check: A season or promo date sits inside the sea transit window for a heavy or bulky SKU, and the PO has not gone out.

risk.note: A timing decision.

prerequisites: The season calendar
Total lead time for the lane (F2)
steps: Identify SKUs where air freight cost per unit is material against landed cost.
Set the PO date at least total lead time days before the stock must be on the PDP.
Check the date against the season calendar before confirming the order.
Escalate to the owner if the timeline cannot fit sea freight.

test.method: Check the PO date against the required land date for every heavy or bulky SKU.
test.measure: Share of heavy-item POs placed within the sea transit window
test.read_point: Before each seasonal or promo order

title: Choose a freight forwarder on service and reliability, not the lowest quote
hypothesis: If a freight forwarder is chosen on sailing date reliability and whether the load waits for container consolidation, not the cheapest quote, then a shipment does not sit at port waiting to fill a container, because that wait is a missed promo for a small saving.

signal.check: A forwarder is picked mainly on the lowest quote, with no check on whether the load waits for consolidation.

risk.note: A selection criterion, not a new cost.

prerequisites: Multiple forwarder quotes for the lane
steps: Get quotes from at least 2 forwarders for the lane.
Ask each for the sailing date and whether the load waits for consolidation.
Weigh service and reliability alongside price when choosing.
Record the choice and reasoning for future shipments.

test.method: Track actual transit days versus quoted transit days by forwarder.
test.measure: Actual versus quoted transit days per forwarder
test.read_point: After each shipment with this forwarder

title: Verify a recommended cross-border 3PL independently before switching lanes
hypothesis: If a cross-border fulfilment provider's transit days and cost are checked independently before switching, then a recommendation from a source with a financial interest in the provider does not get taken at face value, because that source discloses being an investor in the provider it names.

signal.check: A cross-border 3PL is being considered on a recommendation from a source with a disclosed financial interest, with no independent check.

risk.note: A verification step before any commitment.

steps: Identify any 3PL or fulfilment recommendation that comes with a disclosed financial interest.
Get independent transit days and cost per order for the lane.
Compare against the current 3PL's actual performance.
Move volume only after the independent numbers confirm the claim.

test.method: Compare independently verified transit days and cost against the recommended provider's claims.
test.measure: Actual transit days and cost per order versus claimed
test.read_point: Before moving any volume to the recommended provider

title: Check the customs de minimis threshold before choosing a cross-border DTC lane
hypothesis: If the de minimis or small-parcel customs threshold and who pays duty at the door are checked before choosing a cross-border direct-to-customer lane, then a surprise duty charge does not turn into a refused parcel and a refund, because the threshold changes both the landed cost math and the paperwork.

signal.check: A cross-border direct fulfilment lane is being chosen with no current check on the destination's duty threshold.

risk.note: A research step before committing to a lane.

steps: Look up the current de minimis or small-parcel customs threshold for the destination lane.
Confirm who pays duty at the door for parcels above the threshold.
Factor the answer into the landed cost math for that lane.
Disclose any expected duty at checkout to avoid a refused parcel.

test.method: Track refused parcels or refunds tied to unexpected duty on this lane.
test.measure: Refused-parcel and refund rate on the cross-border lane
test.read_point: After the first month running the lane

title: Let a luxury or considered-purchase SKU carry slow freight and longer terms
hypothesis: If a luxury or considered-purchase SKU is allowed to use slow sea freight and longer supplier terms, then cash is not spent rushing a purchase cycle that customers do not rush either, because the SKU's own purchase behaviour can tolerate the wait.
does_not_apply_when: A low-AOV impulse SKU (see COG-075).

signal.check: A luxury or considered-purchase SKU is being defaulted to fast, expensive freight and short terms like the rest of the catalogue.

risk.note: A policy choice by SKU type.

prerequisites: The SKU's AOV and typical purchase cycle
steps: Identify SKUs that are luxury or considered purchases by AOV and repeat cycle.
Default those SKUs to sea freight instead of air.
Negotiate longer payment terms for these SKUs given the slower sell-through.
Note the AOV and cycle on the freight plan and terms proposal.

test.method: Compare freight cost per unit and float days for these SKUs against fast-turnover SKUs.
test.measure: Freight cost per unit and float days by SKU type
test.read_point: At the next freight and terms review

title: Give a low-AOV impulse SKU fast freight and avoid deep cash-locking volume tiers
hypothesis: If a low-AOV impulse SKU is given fast fulfilment and kept out of the deepest volume-discount tier, then the brand avoids locking cash it cannot carry for a fast-moving, low-margin SKU, because that SKU cannot tolerate the cash lock-up of the deepest tier.
does_not_apply_when: A luxury or high-AOV considered-purchase SKU (see COG-074).

signal.check: A low-AOV impulse SKU is being sourced at the deepest volume tier or on a slow freight mode, the same as the rest of the catalogue.

risk.note: A policy choice by SKU type.

prerequisites: The SKU's AOV and repeat cycle
steps: Identify low-AOV impulse SKUs by AOV and repeat cycle.
Prioritise fast freight modes for these SKUs to match their fast purchase cycle.
Avoid the deepest volume-discount tier if it locks more cash than the SKU's margin supports.
Note the AOV and cycle on the freight plan and the F8 table.

test.method: Compare days of cover and cash locked for these SKUs against the store's cash tolerance.
test.measure: Days of cover and cash locked at the chosen tier
test.read_point: Before choosing a volume tier for these SKUs

title: Choose a 3PL on documented accuracy, speed, communication and Q4 surge history
hypothesis: If a 3PL is chosen on documented order error rate, peak processing speed, a named contact and prior Q4 surge history, never on price or promises, then a peak-season failure is less likely, because a 3PL failure at peak is a checkout failure, not just a warehouse problem.

signal.check: A 3PL is being chosen or renewed mainly on price, with no documented error rate, speed or surge history.

expected_effect.size: one self-reported Q4 collapse cost tens of millions against a $45M to $50M forecast

risk.note: An evaluation step before committing.

prerequisites: Order volume and peak forecast
The store's platform and warehouse tool stack
steps: Ask each candidate for order error rate, peak processing speed and method, a named direct contact and documented prior Q4 surges for other brands.
Ask how they handle returns, damages and restocks, and whether they flag issues proactively.
Name the store platform explicitly and ask for order sync and out-of-stock sync to the storefront.
Score and document every answer instead of accepting a verbal promise.

test.method: Run a test order that syncs stock back to the storefront before signing.
test.measure: Documented error rate and sync accuracy in the test order
test.read_point: Before signing, and again before the next peak season

title: Visit a candidate 3PL's warehouse in person before signing
hypothesis: If the owner or a partner visits 2 or 3 candidate warehouses in person, then the real operators stand out from the ones that only sound good on a call, because a physical visit surfaces problems a phone screen cannot.

signal.check: A 3PL decision is close with no in-person warehouse visit done for any candidate.

risk.note: Travel time and cost; low risk otherwise.

prerequisites: A shortlist of 2 to 3 candidate 3PLs
steps: Shortlist 2 to 3 candidate 3PLs on documented criteria (COG-076).
Schedule an in-person visit to each warehouse.
Observe how orders are actually processed, not just how the tour is presented.
Score and compare after all visits are done, before signing.

test.method: Compare pre-visit impressions against post-visit findings for each candidate.
test.measure: Number of red flags found on visit versus on the sales call
test.read_point: After the warehouse visits, before signing

title: Ask a candidate 3PL how it handles returns, damages and restocks
hypothesis: If a candidate 3PL is asked specifically how it handles returns, damages and restocks, and whether it flags issues proactively, then a gap in their process shows up before it becomes a customer-facing problem, because these are the failure points a generic sales pitch skips over.

signal.check: A 3PL evaluation has covered speed and accuracy but not the specific returns, damage and restock process.

risk.note: A diligence question.

steps: Ask each candidate to walk through their returns process step by step.
Ask how damaged goods are handled and reported.
Ask how restocks are triggered and confirmed.
Ask whether they flag issues proactively or wait to be asked.

test.method: Compare answers against actual performance once live.
test.measure: Match between stated process and observed process
test.read_point: In the first 90 days of the relationship

title: Track 3PL inventory turnover weekly and hold a monthly review
hypothesis: If inventory turnover is tracked weekly on a shared dashboard with the warehouse and a monthly review is held, then a drift between the 3PL's stock count and the storefront's count is caught early, because ongoing management, not just initial selection, keeps a 3PL relationship healthy.

signal.check: A 3PL relationship is running with no shared dashboard or scheduled review.

risk.note: A recurring management task.

prerequisites: An active 3PL relationship
steps: Set up a shared dashboard showing on-hand per SKU at the 3PL.
Check it against the storefront's own stock count weekly.
Hold a monthly review with the 3PL on turnover, errors and any process changes.
Tighten the review cadence in the weeks before a peak season.

test.method: Check the dashboard's stock count against the storefront's count each week.
test.measure: Stock count discrepancy, weekly
test.read_point: Every week, tightened before peak

title: Set a computed reorder point per SKU from velocity, lead time and safety stock
hypothesis: If the reorder point per SKU is computed as daily sales velocity times total lead time plus safety stock, and the SKU reorders when on hand plus on order falls to it, then stockouts and excess stock both drop, because the trigger is based on real velocity and lead time, not a guess.

signal.check: A stocked SKU has no computed reorder point, only a manual or gut-feel reorder trigger.

expected_effect.size: one worked example: 50 units per day times 60 days plus 500 safety stock equals a 3,500-unit reorder point

risk.note: A calculation change to the reorder process.

prerequisites: Daily units sold per SKU from the order history
On-hand and on-order units per SKU
Measured total lead time (F2)
steps: Compute daily sales velocity per SKU from the order history, over a window long enough to smooth noise (F3).
Compute total lead time per SKU from measured shipment history (F2).
Set safety stock per SKU from the owner's safety days (F5).
Compute the reorder point as velocity times lead time plus safety stock (F4).
Trigger a reorder review when on hand plus on order falls to or below this point.

test.method: Track whether reorders trigger before a stockout across a sample of SKUs.
test.measure: Stockout days per SKU after the reorder point is in place
test.read_point: Over the following 2 to 3 reorder cycles

title: Run a named weekly review of velocity, lead time and stock position
hypothesis: If one named person runs a weekly review of velocity, lead time and stock position, then a demand spike is caught before it sells out the PDP, because a spike sells out a listing before the next PO can land if nobody is watching.

signal.check: No named person reviews velocity, lead time and stock position on a weekly cadence.

expected_effect.size: one self-reported case: no forecasting during a demand spike led to a sellout within a week and about 2 months unable to fill orders

risk.note: An ownership and cadence assignment.

prerequisites: The reorder point calculation running (COG-080)
steps: Name one person to own the weekly stock review, whatever the team size.
Refresh velocity, flag slow movers and spikes every week.
Update lead times from the last landed shipment.
Re-run the reorder point and log the review with a date.

test.method: Check whether a dated weekly review log exists with a named owner.
test.measure: Weeks with a completed, logged review
test.read_point: Every week

title: Size safety stock from the brand's own spike and delay risk
hypothesis: If safety stock per SKU is set from the brand's own observed spike and delay risk, highest for a SKU with paid traffic pointed at it, then the buffer matches real risk instead of a guess, because a stockout on an advertised SKU wastes committed ad spend.

signal.check: Safety stock is a round guessed number with no link to the SKU's own spike history or ad spend level.

risk.note: A sizing input the owner sets.

prerequisites: Owner's stockout tolerance
Observed lead-time variance per SKU
steps: Ask the owner for the acceptable safety days per SKU, or a direct unit figure.
Set the days higher for any SKU carrying live ad spend.
Compute safety stock as safety days times daily sales velocity (F5).
Record the reason for the chosen safety days next to the number.

test.method: Track stockouts on ad-spend SKUs versus their safety stock level.
test.measure: Stockout days for SKUs with higher versus lower safety stock
test.read_point: Over the following quarter

title: Send suppliers the sales forecast before problems appear
hypothesis: If the sales forecast and stock position are shared with suppliers weekly, and whenever a promo moves the forecast, then a supplier has time to react before a shortage hits, because telling a supplier about a problem after it appears is too late to fix it.

signal.check: A promo or ad push that changes the forecast has gone on the calendar, but the supplier has not been told.

risk.note: A communication habit.

prerequisites: A current demand forecast per SKU
steps: Send the current forecast and stock position to each active supplier weekly.
Send an update immediately when a promo or ad push materially changes the forecast.
Confirm the supplier acknowledges the change.
Log the message and date sent.

test.method: Check whether the forecast sent matches the demand plan on file.
test.measure: Match between forecast sent and demand plan
test.read_point: Weekly, or whenever the forecast changes

title: Write a demand plan before any non-routine purchase order
hypothesis: If every non-routine PO gets a written demand plan covering velocity, seasonal view, days of cover, cash locked, defect buffer and lead time, then the order size is grounded in real numbers, because a launch or promo already committed for the SKU needs more than trailing velocity to size correctly.

signal.check: A PO larger than a routine reorder is being placed with no written demand plan behind it.

risk.note: A planning step before commitment.

prerequisites: The reorder calendar (COG-080)
The quote comparison (COG-023)
The defect buffer (COG-062)
steps: State demand units for the horizon using velocity times the days of cover wanted, adjusted for any planned channel push.
Compute order units with the defect buffer added (F7).
Show cash at deposit, cash total, days of cover and landed cost for the chosen tier (F8), plus float (F1).
Check the margin gate (COG-026) before finalising.
Attach the plan to the PO draft.

test.method: Check every non-routine PO has an attached demand plan with all fields filled.
test.measure: Share of non-routine POs with a complete demand plan attached
test.read_point: Before every non-routine PO

title: Size a non-routine order from the committed channel push, not trailing velocity alone
hypothesis: If demand units for a non-routine order reflect the channel plan already committed for that SKU, not only trailing velocity, then sourcing does not under-order into a planned spike, because a launch or ad push moves demand before the sales history shows it.

signal.check: A demand plan is being built from trailing velocity alone while a marketing push for the same SKU is already committed.

risk.note: A demand sizing adjustment.

prerequisites: The committed channel or ad plan for the SKU
The demand plan process (COG-084)
steps: Pull the committed channel plan and media dollars for the SKU from the marketing calendar.
Adjust demand units upward from trailing velocity to reflect the planned push.
Flag the adjustment as channel-driven, separate from organic trend.
Re-check after the push runs and compare actual against planned demand.

test.method: Compare stockout incidence on channel-adjusted orders versus velocity-only orders.
test.measure: Stockout days for SKUs with a channel-adjusted demand plan
test.read_point: During and after the planned push

title: Put every required field in the PO draft so nothing is left to the factory
hypothesis: If the PO draft states spec version, quantity with buffer, price and tier, deposit and balance terms with the QC condition, incoterm, freight mode, ship date, packaging spec, inspection details and payment route, then nothing is left for the factory to decide, because an unwritten field is a decision left to the factory.

signal.check: A PO draft has a blank field where a number, date or condition should be.

risk.note: A documentation completeness check.

prerequisites: Spec version and approved sample ids
Quote, sample sign-off, terms and freight plan all complete
steps: List every required field: SKU and version, quantity with buffer, unit price and tier, price-break thresholds and credits.
Add deposit and balance split with the QC-pass condition, incoterm and freight mode.
Add production days, required ship date, packaging spec, inspection date and provider, and payment route.
Block the draft from moving forward if any field is blank.

test.method: Check every field is filled before the draft goes to the owner.
test.measure: Share of PO drafts with zero blank fields
test.read_point: Before every PO is sent to the owner for approval

title: Flag a below-reorder-point SKU on the PDP and throttle its ad spend
hypothesis: If a SKU that falls below its reorder point gets a sold-out or back-in-stock-soon PDP state and a flag to throttle its ad spend, then ad budget stops chasing clicks that cannot convert, because paid traffic on a stocked-out SKU is wasted spend the moment days of cover drops under lead time.

signal.check: A SKU's on-hand plus on-order has fallen below its reorder point, or days of cover has dropped under total lead time, with no PDP or ad change.

risk.note: A pacing and PDP-state rule.

prerequisites: The reorder point calculation (COG-080)
Ad campaign access for the SKU
steps: Set an automatic check for on-hand plus on-order against the reorder point.
When it falls below, change the PDP to sold out or back in stock soon rather than hiding the listing.
Send a flag to marketing or ad ops the same day.
Throttle ad spend on that SKU until stock is confirmed inbound.

test.method: Track ad spend and CPA on flagged SKUs before and after the throttle.
test.measure: Wasted spend on out-of-stock clicks, before versus after
test.read_point: On every trigger event

title: Size a subscription SKU's reorder point from committed cadence, not trailing sales
hypothesis: If a subscription SKU's reorder point and order quantity add the committed subscriber cadence as a floor to the trailing-velocity calculation, then the order size reflects real, contracted demand, because a one-off purchase SKU can rely on velocity alone but a subscription SKU has committed volume ahead of it.
does_not_apply_when: A one-off purchase SKU with no recurring commitment.

signal.check: A subscription SKU's reorder point is computed from trailing daily sales velocity only, with no add for committed subscriber volume.

risk.note: A calculation adjustment.

prerequisites: The reorder point calculation (COG-080)
Committed subscriber units for the next lead-time window
steps: Pull committed subscriber units due to ship within the next lead-time window.
Add that figure as a floor to the standard reorder point calculation (F4).
Recompute whenever the subscriber base changes materially.
Flag any gap between committed units and available stock.

test.method: Compare stockouts on subscription SKUs before and after adding the committed-cadence floor.
test.measure: Stockout days and missed subscription shipments
test.read_point: Over the following 2 reorder cycles

title: Build the demand plan from bundle sell-through, not single-unit history
hypothesis: If a component sold mainly inside a bundle or kit gets its demand plan from the kit's own sell-through times its contents, then component ordering matches how it actually sells, because a kit's component units follow the kit's sell-through, not each component's own separate history.
does_not_apply_when: A component that also sells heavily on its own, outside any bundle.

signal.check: A bundle or kit component's demand plan is built from its own standalone sales history, ignoring the kit's sell-through.

risk.note: A calculation adjustment.

prerequisites: Kit or bundle sell-through data
The bill of materials for the kit's contents
steps: Identify every SKU sold mainly as part of a bundle or kit.
Pull the kit's own sell-through velocity, not the component's standalone history.
Multiply kit units by the kit's contents per component to get component demand.
Feed this into the standard demand plan (COG-084) for that component.

test.method: Check component units in the plan equal kit units times kit contents.
test.measure: Match between planned component units and kit-derived units
test.read_point: At every demand plan update for a bundled SKU

title: Round the order quantity up to the supplier's carton or MOQ multiple
hypothesis: If the computed order quantity, including the defect buffer, is rounded up to the supplier's carton or MOQ multiple, and the rounding is shown, then the PO reflects what can actually be produced and shipped, because an unrounded number the factory has to adjust reintroduces the exact guesswork the demand plan was built to avoid.

signal.check: A PO's order quantity is an exact demand-plan number that does not divide evenly into the supplier's carton size or MOQ.

risk.note: A rounding step in the calculation.

prerequisites: The order quantity with defect buffer (COG-062)
The supplier's carton size or MOQ multiple
steps: Take the order quantity computed with the defect buffer (F7).
Round up to the nearest multiple of the supplier's carton size or MOQ.
Show both the pre-rounding and post-rounding number on the PO draft.
Confirm the rounded quantity still fits the cash and cover plan (F8).

test.method: Check every PO shows both the raw and rounded quantity.
test.measure: Share of POs with rounding shown
test.read_point: On every PO draft

title: Compute and flag supplier concentration share
hypothesis: If the share of annual COGS with a single supplier is computed from the BOM and flagged when large, then the store treats it as a risk to manage, because a concentrated supplier failing during a scheduled promo does more damage than the same failure in a slow month.

signal.check: A single supplier's share of annual COGS has never been computed, or a large share exists with no mitigation plan.

expected_effect.size: one case had about 70% of COGS with 1 supplier, treated as a risk to manage

risk.note: An analysis step.

prerequisites: A BOM with cost and supplier per component (COG-004)
steps: Sum component cost times annual units for each supplier across the BOM.
Divide by total annual COGS to get each supplier's share (F11).
Flag any share the owner considers too large.
Weigh the flag against the marketing calendar, since a concentrated supplier failing during a scheduled promo does more damage.

test.method: Refresh the concentration share at each BOM review and track the trend.
test.measure: Supplier concentration share over time
test.read_point: At each yearly BOM review (COG-043)

title: Compute and flag country concentration share
hypothesis: If the share of annual COGS tied to components from a single country is computed and flagged, then a tariff or trade disruption in that country is planned for as a stockout risk, not only a cost risk, because a single-country shock breaks the chain, not just the margin.

signal.check: A single country's share of annual COGS has never been computed from the BOM's country-of-origin column.

risk.note: An analysis step.

prerequisites: A BOM with country of origin per component (COG-004)
steps: Sum component cost times annual units for each country of origin in the BOM.
Divide by total annual COGS to get each country's share (F11).
Flag any single country carrying a large share.
Use the flag to prioritise the backup-country mapping (COG-093).

test.method: Refresh the country share at each BOM review and track the trend.
test.measure: Country concentration share over time
test.read_point: At each yearly BOM review (COG-043)

title: Map a backup factory in a second country before it's needed
hypothesis: If at least one backup factory is mapped in a second country even at zero current volume, then a single-country disruption does not break the supply chain, because building a contingency during a crisis is too slow to help.

signal.check: The entire supply chain for a category runs through a single country with no mapped backup elsewhere.

risk.note: A vetting cost for a backup that may see zero volume for a long time.

prerequisites: A candidate second country identified
steps: Identify a candidate country different from the current source's country.
Vet at least one factory there through the shortlist process (COG-013 to COG-016).
Get it to a passed sample even at zero committed volume.
Record the backup's country in the supplier record, distinct from the incumbent's.

test.method: Check the backup's country differs from the incumbent's on the supplier record.
test.measure: Whether a second-country backup with a passed sample exists
test.read_point: Before peak season, or once a year

title: Score a candidate sourcing country on 4 qualitative factors
hypothesis: If a candidate country is scored on raw material origin, labor cost, overall taxes and development trajectory, then a diversification decision starts from a written comparison instead of a guess, because an unknown factor makes the whole estimate unreliable.

signal.check: A country diversification idea is being discussed with no written comparison on the 4 factors.

risk.note: A research and scoring step.

prerequisites: A list of candidate countries
steps: List candidate countries for the category.
Record raw material origin, labor cost, overall taxes and development trajectory for each.
Mark any factor that is unknown rather than guessing at it.
Decide with the owner whether speed or cost matters more for this product.

test.method: Check every candidate has all 4 factors recorded or marked incomplete.
test.measure: Share of candidates with a complete 4-factor score
test.read_point: Before recommending any country move

title: Run the lead-time versus cost trade-off with real quotes before moving production
hypothesis: If the lead-time and cost change for a candidate country is computed from real quotes and forwarder transit days, not an illustration, then a relocation decision is grounded in the brand's own numbers, because one illustrative example showed lead time up about 30% against cost down about 30%, a trade-off that varies by lane.

signal.check: A country relocation is being considered using an illustrative example from a source instead of real quotes for the brand's own product.

expected_effect.size: unknown, varies by lane; one illustration showed lead time about plus 30% and cost about minus 30%

risk.note: A quote-gathering and calculation step.

prerequisites: Real quotes from at least 1 factory in the candidate country
Forwarder transit days for the new lane
Duty rate for the candidate's origin
steps: Get a real quote from at least 1 factory in the candidate country.
Get forwarder transit days for the new lane.
Compute lead-time change percent and cost change percent versus the current country (F12).
Add the safety stock and days-of-cover impact of the longer or shorter lane.

test.method: Compare the computed trade-off against the actual result after any move.
test.measure: Lead-time and cost change percent, projected versus actual
test.read_point: Before the move, then again after the first shipment from the new country

title: Hold volume flat and ask for a concession when a shock breaks margin
hypothesis: If unit economics break from a tariff, duty or commodity move, the brand holds volume flat rather than growing into broken margins, and asks for a temporary concession where the BOM shows an abnormal supplier margin, then the SKU is protected until the shock eases, because pushing growth into broken margins compounds the loss.

signal.check: A duty, tariff or commodity move has pushed landed cost past the margin gate on a SKU with live ad spend.

expected_effect.size: one case paused growth about 1 year during a roughly 50% tariff period and got a concession from a supplier running about 25 to 35% margin

risk.note: Pausing growth has an opportunity cost, but growing into broken margins costs more.

prerequisites: Landed cost recomputed with the new rate (COG-025)
Country-of-origin BOM data (COG-004)
steps: Recompute landed cost with the duty or spot price actually paid, not the old rate.
If the margin gate fails, hold the ad and growth budget flat on that SKU, do not pull the listing.
Check the BOM for an abnormal supplier margin for the category and ask for a temporary concession.
Plan to give some margin back once the shock eases, and start a country diversification review (COG-094) for the long term.

test.method: Track margin recovery and ad spend pacing on the affected SKU through the shock.
test.measure: Gross margin and ad spend on the SKU, before, during and after the shock
test.read_point: At the shock, then monthly until margin recovers

title: Weigh a cost-down push against a CAC push using the real BOM
hypothesis: If a mature brand with a real BOM compares a cost-down round against a CAC-focused push using actual numbers, then the budget goes where the BOM shows real room, because a placed PO cannot be cancelled the way ad spend can, so a cost-down mistake locks in longer.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with no BOM yet; build the BOM first (COG-004).

signal.check: A budget decision between a cost-down push and a CAC push is being made without checking the BOM for real cost-down room.

expected_effect.size: unknown, 1 operator's view against mainstream CAC-first advice

risk.note: A prioritisation decision.

prerequisites: A component-level BOM (COG-004)
steps: Review the BOM for lines with real, provable cost-down room.
Compare the expected COGS saving against the expected return from an equivalent CAC investment.
State the claim as one operator's view, not a universal rule, when presenting it.
Only count a cost-down as real once the invoice reconciliation (COG-041) confirms it.

test.method: Track whether a chosen cost-down round shows up on invoices within the expected timeframe.
test.measure: Confirmed cost-down amount versus projected CAC-push return
test.read_point: One quarter after the budget decision

title: Decide whether a full component BOM is worth building given the SKU's COGS size
hypothesis: If the decision to build a full component-level BOM weighs the SKU's or brand's annual COGS size, then sourcing effort goes to where the negotiating room is large enough to justify it, because building a detailed BOM takes real time that a small SKU may not repay.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with a hero SKU carrying ad spend, where R74 applies regardless of COGS size.

signal.check: A decision to invest in a full component-level BOM is being made without checking the SKU's or brand's annual COGS against a size threshold.

expected_effect.size: one operator's own judgment put the threshold around $1M per year of COGS, or about $2.5M revenue for some businesses; not a general rule

risk.note: A prioritisation decision, not a commitment.

prerequisites: Annual COGS or revenue estimate for the SKU or brand
steps: Estimate the SKU's or brand's annual COGS.
Compare against the brand's own threshold for when a full BOM effort pays off.
For a SKU below the threshold, keep the tech pack level of detail (COG-003) without a full component BOM.
Revisit the decision as the SKU or brand scales.

test.method: Track time spent on BOM building against the COGS the BOM actually informed a negotiation on.
test.measure: Hours spent on BOM work versus COGS saving achieved
test.read_point: After the first cost-down attempt using the BOM

title: Recompute landed cost whenever price, freight, FX or duty changes
hypothesis: If landed cost per unit is recomputed every time price, freight, exchange rate or duty changes, then pricing and margin decisions never run on a stale number, because a landed cost from months ago can be wrong the moment any one input moves.

signal.check: The landed cost table's effective date is older than the last known change in price, freight, FX or duty.

risk.note: A recalculation step.

prerequisites: The landed cost calculation in place (COG-025)
steps: Watch for a change in factory price, freight rate, exchange rate or duty rate.
Recompute landed cost per unit as soon as any one input changes (F6).
Version the table with the new effective date.
Flag the change to pricing and ad-spend decisions that depend on it.

test.method: Check the landed cost table's effective date against the date of the last known input change.
test.measure: Days between an input change and the landed cost recompute
test.read_point: Whenever a price, freight, FX or duty change is known

title: Run a full sourcing audit in the first week of a takeover or new client
hypothesis: If a new client or acquired brand gets a sourcing audit in the first week covering the BOM, concentration, COGS trend, terms, sample logs and reorder method, then the biggest sourcing gaps are known before any negotiation or promo commitment, because acting without this picture risks repeating the brand's existing mistakes.

signal.check: A new client or acquired brand has started work with no sourcing audit completed in the first week.

risk.note: A diagnostic step before any commitment is made.

prerequisites: Access to the brand's supplier, quote, sample and inventory records
steps: Ask for the BOM; if none exists, building it is the first task (COG-004).
Compute concentration and country shares (COG-091, COG-092).
Ask when COGS last declined on each mature SKU (COG-011).
Check terms, float and payment route per supplier (COG-050).
Review sample logs and inspection history.
Check the reorder method in use and the date of the last stockout.
Hand the gap list to the owner with a recommended order of work.

test.method: Check the audit's gap list is delivered within the first week and each gap is later addressed or accepted.
test.measure: Days to deliver the audit, and gaps closed within the following quarter
test.read_point: End of week 1, then quarterly

title: Automate purchase orders from weekly to daily at high SKU count
hypothesis: If a catalogue with thousands of SKUs moves purchase order placement from a weekly manual cycle to a daily rules-based one, then replenishment reacts to real sell-through faster, because a weekly cycle cannot keep up with SKU-level demand swings at that scale.
does_not_apply_when: A SKU count small enough that one person can review every reorder point weekly without falling behind.

signal.check: The SKU count is large enough that the weekly PO review is late or skips SKUs, and a below-reorder-point SKU sits unordered for days before the next weekly cycle runs.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the source describes the switch but gives no measured stockout change

risk.note: A wrong rule can over-order or under-order many SKUs at once; keep human approval on early runs.

prerequisites: A computed reorder point per SKU from velocity, lead time and safety stock
A catalogue large enough that weekly manual review is the actual bottleneck
Someone who can write or commission the daily replenishment logic
steps: List every SKU's reorder point, lead time and MOQ so the daily logic has real inputs.
Write the rule the system should follow: draft a PO when on hand plus on order falls to the reorder point.
Build or commission software that checks this rule daily instead of waiting for the weekly cycle.
Route each daily draft PO to a person for approval before it sends, at least at first.
Compare stockouts and excess stock in the first month against the prior weekly-cycle baseline.
Widen the rule to more SKUs once daily drafts match what a manual review would have ordered.

test.method: Run daily automated PO drafts alongside the existing weekly process for one full replenishment cycle before switching over.
test.measure: Stockout days per SKU, excess stock value, hours spent on manual PO review
test.read_point: After one full lead-time cycle on daily POs

title: Base a sourcing operator near key suppliers to build terms faster
hypothesis: If the person who owns supplier relationships is based near the manufacturing hub instead of visiting occasionally, then face time with the factory rises, because more interaction frequency is the mechanism a near-supplier base gives you for building trust and negotiating terms.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with one or two annual orders where the travel cost is not worth the relationship gain.

signal.check: Supplier visits happen less than once a year, terms have not moved in years, and every negotiation is done remotely by chat or email.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the source claims a relationship advantage from proximity but gives no measured cost change

risk.note: Relocating a person is a real cost and lifestyle decision; treat it as a considered move, not a quick test.

prerequisites: A core supplier concentrated in one region worth the relationship investment
A team member willing and able to relocate near that hub
steps: Identify the single hub where the core supplier or the category's best factories sit.
Weigh relocating a sourcing owner there against the cost of frequent trips instead.
If relocating, set a visit cadence with the factory that a remote relationship could not sustain.
Use the face time to build the relationship before asking for a price break, not only during a negotiation.
Track whether visit frequency correlates with faster sample turnaround or better terms over the following year.

test.method: Compare sample turnaround time, response time and any price or term movement in the 12 months after the move against the 12 months before.
test.measure: Sample turnaround days, cogs_per_unit change, supplier_lead_days
test.read_point: 12 months after relocation or after the new visit cadence starts

title: Open a new market with one cross-border 3PL hub and one global ad set
hypothesis: If a light, small product is stocked in one cross-border 3PL hub and one Meta ad set carries the best-performing creatives to every shippable country, then international sales can start without building country-by-country fulfilment first, because the fulfilment side of expansion is solved once, before any localization work.
does_not_apply_when: A heavy or bulky product where cross-border shipping cost erases the margin.
A store not yet profitable in its home market.

signal.check: The product is small and light enough to ship affordably from one hub, the home market is already profitable, and no international campaign exists yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the source frames this as a simple first step, not a measured lift

risk.note: One ad set and one 3PL contract can be paused or ended if the countries do not perform.

prerequisites: A light, low-cost-to-ship product
A profitable home-market campaign with proven creatives
A cross-border 3PL that can hold and ship light inventory internationally
steps: Confirm the product is light enough to ship affordably from a single international hub.
Place a small batch of inventory with a cross-border 3PL in that hub.
Build one new global campaign with one ad set loaded with the best-performing home-market creatives.
Add every country you can ship to at a reasonable landed cost to that one ad set.
Run in the home market's language first; leave localization for a later phase.
Read results by country after enough spend to judge them, then cut or scale each one.

test.method: Run the single global ad set for at least 2 to 4 weeks and read results split by country.
test.measure: roas_blended and sessions by country, landed shipping cost per order
test.read_point: After the first 2 to 4 weeks of the global ad set

title: Re-quote competing factories on a schedule even for a happy supplier
hypothesis: If competing quotes are pulled on a fixed schedule even when the current supplier relationship is good, then pricing stays honest over time, because a long, quiet relationship with no outside comparison is exactly when a factory is most likely to let its price drift.
does_not_apply_when: A supplier already re-quoted this year through a separate cost-down or BOM review.

signal.check: No competing quote has been pulled for a core SKU's supplier in the last 12 months, even though the relationship is stable and happy.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source gives no measured saving for this specific practice

risk.note: Getting a quote does not commit you to switching; frame it to the current supplier as market checking, not a threat.

prerequisites: A list of core suppliers and the date each was last re-quoted
steps: Set a fixed cadence, such as once or twice a year, to re-quote every core supplier.
Request quotes from 2 to 3 alternate factories on the same spec, quantity and terms.
Tell the current supplier directly that you are getting outside quotes, framed as routine, not a threat.
Compare the outside quotes against the current price and terms.
Bring any real gap to the current supplier as a chance to match, before switching anything.
Log the result and the next scheduled re-quote date regardless of outcome.

test.method: Track whether a scheduled re-quote round finds a price or term gap versus the current supplier.
test.measure: cogs_per_unit before and after the round, number of rounds that found a gap
test.read_point: At each scheduled re-quote date

title: Check IP and trademark exposure before reverse engineering a reference sample
hypothesis: If a reference item is checked for trademark or IP ownership before it is sent to a factory to be reverse engineered, then the store avoids building a product spec on something it has no right to copy, because sending someone else's branded product to a factory as a copy target is itself the exposure.
does_not_apply_when: The reference item is the brand's own prior product or one it has clear rights to copy.

signal.check: A reference sample used to brief a factory is a competitor's or another brand's branded product, and no one has checked whether copying it creates trademark or design risk.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source flags the risk but gives no measured outcome

risk.note: Once a spec built on a copied branded item reaches production and sale, the exposure cannot be undone by stopping the check later.

prerequisites: The reference sample in hand
Someone able to check the item's brand, patents or registered design
steps: Identify the brand or origin of every reference sample before it is sent to a factory.
If the item carries a visible brand, logo or known design, flag it before using it as a copy target.
Ask whether the factory brief can specify materials and construction without literally copying a branded design.
Get a quick legal read on real risk when the item is a well-known branded product.
Keep a record of which reference samples were checked and the outcome.

test.method: Review every reference sample against this check before it is sent to a factory, and log the review.
test.measure: Share of reference samples with a documented IP check before use
test.read_point: At each new product brief

title: Use an easy-iteration location to test, then move scaled production to a hub
hypothesis: If early product testing and small runs happen in a location chosen for easy access and fast iteration, while scaled production moves to an established manufacturing hub, then the store gets fast early testing without carrying that location's higher scale cost, because a location good for testing small batches is not necessarily good for scaled cost or lead time.
does_not_apply_when: A brand whose test location is already an established, low-cost manufacturing hub for its category.

signal.check: Production is still running in a location chosen for early convenience even though most raw material is imported from elsewhere, labor cost is relatively high, or holidays and downtime slow output.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source gives no measured comparison, only a stated intent to move production out

risk.note: Moving scaled production is a real transition; keep the test location's supplier as a backup during the move.

prerequisites: A test location already used for small runs
A shortlisted established hub for the category
steps: List what the current test location is actually good for: fast iteration, fabric or material access, small runs.
List where its costs work against scale: import reliance, relative labor cost, holiday or downtime patterns.
Identify an established manufacturing hub for the category with lower scale cost or better lead time.
Move production for any SKU that has passed testing to the established hub, keeping the test location for new development.
Compare landed cost and lead time on the moved SKU before and after.

test.method: Run the same SKU's landed cost and lead time from both locations before fully moving scaled volume.
test.measure: cogs_per_unit, supplier_lead_days
test.read_point: After the first production run from the new hub

title: Hire a freelance designer to build the tech pack when design skill is missing
hypothesis: If a store without in-house design skill hires a freelance product designer to build the tech pack instead of skipping or writing it in-house, then a complete, professional spec reaches the factory, because a missing design skill should not be the reason a spec ships with open points.
does_not_apply_when: A team that already has a designer capable of producing a complete tech pack in-house.

signal.check: No one on the team can produce drawings, measurements and colourways to spec, and the current tech pack is thin or missing.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source gives a cost example for the hire, not a measured return-rate change

risk.note: A single freelance project with a clear brief and reference photos is low commitment.

prerequisites: Product drawings, reference photos or a physical sample to brief the designer
A freelance marketplace or referral to find a product designer
steps: Gather reference photos, a physical sample if one exists, and any known measurements.
Post the tech pack brief on a freelance marketplace, naming the required sections: drawings, materials, measurements, colourways, packaging.
Review candidates for prior tech pack or product-design work, not general graphic design.
Have the designer build the full pack, then review it against the physical sample or reference photos line by line.
Store the finished tech pack in the brand's own system as the versioned reference for every future quote and sample.

test.method: Send the freelance-built tech pack to the next new or candidate factory and track spec mismatches on the returned sample.
test.measure: Spec mismatches per sample, cost of the freelance hire
test.read_point: On the first sample built from the new tech pack

title: Order pre-production samples across the size range to confirm grading
hypothesis: If a SKU sold in multiple sizes gets pre-production samples made across the size range instead of only one size, then a proportion error in the size grading is caught before bulk, because checking one size only shows whether that size is right, not whether the grading between sizes is right.
does_not_apply_when: A SKU sold in one size only.

signal.check: A multi-size SKU's sample sign-off has only checked one size, or size-related returns or fit complaints are rising.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source recommends the practice but gives no measured return-rate change

risk.note: Extra sample units cost a little more and add a short delay before bulk, but catch a size problem before it reaches customers.

prerequisites: A tech pack with measurements for every size or variant
A factory able to produce pre-production samples in more than one size
steps: List every size or variant the SKU will ship in.
Request a pre-production sample in at least the smallest, a middle and the largest size.
Measure each sample against the tech pack's per-size measurements.
Compare the proportions between sizes, not only each size against its own target.
Flag and correct any size whose grading is off before approving the run for bulk.

test.method: Check multi-size pre-production samples against the tech pack's grading before every bulk approval.
test.measure: Size-related return rate, review mentions of fit
test.read_point: After the first bulk shipment following the multi-size check

title: Use a general AI chatbot to draft the landed cost category checklist
hypothesis: If a general AI chatbot is prompted to list the hidden landed-cost categories for a product before a landed-cost spreadsheet is built, then fewer cost lines get missed on the first draft, because a chatbot's generic list is a faster starting point than building the checklist from memory.
does_not_apply_when: A brand that already has a complete, tested landed-cost template it reuses.

signal.check: No landed-cost template exists yet, or the current one has missed a real cost line before (freight, duty, insurance, warehousing, fulfilment, platform or transaction fees).

expected_effect.size: unknown, source presents this as a drafting shortcut, not a measured margin change

risk.note: The chatbot output is a starting checklist only; every category must still be verified against real invoices.

prerequisites: Access to a general AI chatbot
A set of real invoices to verify each suggested cost line against
steps: Prompt a general AI chatbot to list the typical hidden landed-cost categories for the product type.
Turn the resulting list into a spreadsheet template with one row per category.
Check every suggested category against real invoices and drop or rename any that do not apply.
Add any category the chatbot missed that the brand's own invoices show.
Reuse the verified template for every SKU going forward.

test.method: Compare the chatbot-drafted checklist against the categories that actually appear on the next full set of invoices for a shipment.
test.measure: Number of real cost categories missing from the first draft
test.read_point: After reconciling the first shipment's invoices against the draft checklist

title: Ask an established supplier for a premium courier upgrade on a large order
hypothesis: If a large order with an established, good supplier relationship comes with a direct ask for a premium courier upgrade instead of the default slower shipping method, then transit time can drop without a separate freight negotiation, because a supplier with a good relationship and a big order has room to offer this that a small or new order would not get.
does_not_apply_when: A new or unproven supplier relationship, or an order too small to justify the ask.

signal.check: An order is large and the supplier relationship is established, but the default shipping method is still the slow standard option and no one has asked about an upgrade.

expected_effect.size: one case went from 10 to 14 days on the default method to 4 to 5 days on the upgrade

risk.note: Asking costs nothing; a refusal simply keeps the default shipping method.

prerequisites: An established supplier relationship
An order large enough to justify the ask
steps: Confirm the order qualifies: a large quantity with a supplier that already has a track record with the brand.
Ask the supplier directly whether they can upgrade this shipment to a premium courier instead of the default method.
Get the revised transit time and any added cost in writing before confirming.
Weigh the added cost against the value of the faster stock arrival for this specific launch or restock.
Record whether the upgrade was granted and the resulting transit time for future orders.

test.method: Compare transit time and added cost on the upgraded shipment against the default method's historical transit time.
test.measure: fulfilment_days, added shipping cost per unit
test.read_point: On arrival of the upgraded shipment

title: Run a five-step hiring sequence from scorecard to reference-checked offer
hypothesis: If every hire goes through scorecard, screening, topgrading, a competency and culture case study, then a reference-checked offer in that order, then hiring becomes comparable across candidates and roles, because a standardized sequence catches gaps that an ad hoc interview process misses.
does_not_apply_when: A very small team hiring a single low-stakes role where the full sequence costs more time than the hire is worth.

signal.check: Hiring decisions are made from an unstructured conversation, past hires have had inflated titles or scope revealed only after starting, and no consistent process runs across candidates for the same role.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source credits this method as central to its own growth from about $50M to $200M but gives no controlled comparison

risk.note: The sequence adds time per hire; scale it down for low-stakes roles rather than skipping structure entirely.

prerequisites: A written scorecard for the role
Someone able to run topgrading interviews and check references
steps: Write the role scorecard first, naming outcomes, real competencies and explicitly irrelevant traits.
Run a short standardized screen against the scorecard for every applicant.
Topgrade candidates who pass screening with a chronological, role-by-role interview.
Give finalists a domain case study with deliberate traps plus a culture-fit questionnaire.
Make any senior offer conditional on 2 to 3 standardized reference calls.
Keep the whole record consistent so every stage reconciles with the last.

test.method: Track hires made through the full sequence against prior hires made without it, over the following 6 to 12 months.
test.measure: 90-day and 1-year retention, manager-rated performance, time to productivity
test.read_point: At 90 days and again at 12 months per hire

title: Write a role scorecard that names required outcomes and irrelevant traits
hypothesis: If a role scorecard names the outcomes the hire must deliver, the real competencies needed and the traits that do not matter, then interviewers judge candidates on the same criteria, because naming what is irrelevant removes the bias of liking a candidate for reasons the role does not need.
does_not_apply_when: A role already filled by someone with a proven track record where no new hire is planned.

signal.check: A role is being hired for with no written outcomes or competency list, and past interviewers for that role disagreed on what made a good candidate.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source gives no measured outcome for the scorecard alone

risk.note: A written document only; no commitment to a candidate yet.

prerequisites: Agreement from everyone involved in hiring on what the role must deliver
steps: List the concrete outcomes the role must produce in its first year.
List the specific competencies needed to produce those outcomes.
Name traits that do not matter for this role, even ones interviewers might personally value.
Share the scorecard with everyone involved in hiring before any interview happens.
Test each candidate's stated career goals against the role's actual growth path.

test.method: Compare interviewer agreement and hire outcomes for roles hired with a scorecard against roles hired without one.
test.measure: Interviewer score agreement, 90-day retention, manager rating
test.read_point: At 90 days after each hire

title: Use standardized screening questions to pre-filter and flag deep-dive topics
hypothesis: If every candidate gets the same short set of probing questions, such as career goals, self-rated manager feedback and role-specific deal-breakers, then weak fits are filtered early and real concerns are flagged for the deeper interview, because a standardized screen surfaces the same signal for every candidate instead of whatever comes up in casual conversation.
does_not_apply_when: A role filled through direct referral where a full screening step would slow down a known, trusted candidate.

signal.check: Candidates move to a full interview with no consistent early screen, and screeners report the same weak fits reaching later stages repeatedly.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source gives no measured outcome for the screen alone

risk.note: A 15 to 20 minute call; low cost per candidate.

prerequisites: A written scorecard so the screening questions map to what the role needs
steps: Write one question per core area: career goals, top strength, top weakness, past-manager rating, and why this company.
Ask the manager-rating question as if calling the manager directly, then push past the first polite answer.
Name role-specific deal-breakers up front, such as disliking a task the role cannot avoid.
Note red flags without resolving them; carry them forward to the deeper interview.
Leave time for the candidate's own questions and leave them with a positive impression regardless of outcome.

test.method: Track how many screened-out candidates would have failed later stages anyway, and how many flagged concerns proved real at topgrading.
test.measure: Screen-to-later-stage drop rate, flagged-concern hit rate
test.read_point: After each hiring round

title: Run a chronological topgrading interview to catch inflated titles
hypothesis: If a finalist candidate is walked chronologically through every role on their resume, asking what they were actually hired to do versus their final title and probing any timeline gap, then an inflated title or a hidden gap surfaces before an offer, because a summary-level interview lets both slide by unquestioned.
does_not_apply_when: A candidate for a short-term or low-stakes role where a bad hire is cheap to reverse.

signal.check: Interviews accept the resume's stated titles and summary at face value, and a past hire's actual scope turned out different from what the title implied.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source gives no measured outcome for this step alone

risk.note: An extended interview only, reserved for candidates who already passed screening.

prerequisites: A candidate who passed initial screening
30 to 60 minutes of interview time
Someone with enough domain knowledge to judge the answers
steps: List every role on the resume in chronological order before the interview.
For each role, ask what they were hired to do, what they actually did, and what results they drove.
Ask about the difference between the title they were hired into and the title they left with.
Probe any gap between roles directly.
Ask who they reported to, their biggest point of pride and their lowest point in each role.

test.method: Compare hires who went through this interview against past hires who did not, on scope match and early performance.
test.measure: Scope-match rate at 90 days, manager rating
test.read_point: At 90 days after the hire starts

title: Test finalist hires with a trapped case study plus a culture questionnaire
lever: case study and culture fit test
hypothesis: If a finalist candidate works a realistic, role-specific case study with deliberate traps using dummy data, then answers a direct culture-fit questionnaire about how the team actually operates, then both competence and fit are tested before an offer, because a general impression from conversation misses both.
does_not_apply_when: A role defined mostly by relationships or judgment calls that a case study cannot simulate.

signal.check: Offers are made on interview impression alone, with no exercise that tests the candidate's actual domain skill or their fit with the team's real operating norms.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source gives no measured outcome for this step alone

risk.note: Use dummy data and a mutual NDA if real materials are shared, so no sensitive data is exposed.

prerequisites: A role-specific case study built with dummy data
A written, honest description of the team's actual operating norms
steps: Build a case study specific to the role, with deliberate traps that test attention to detail and judgment.
Use dummy or fake data so real business information is never exposed.
Have the candidate sign a mutual NDA if any real materials are shared.
Follow the case study with a culture questionnaire that describes your actual daily operating norms, not an idealized version.
Weigh the case study result and the culture answers together before making an offer.

test.method: Compare hires who passed this stage against past hires who did not go through it, on early performance and early attrition.
test.measure: 90-day performance rating, early attrition rate
test.read_point: At 90 days after the hire starts

title: Hire a specialized role in a lower-cost hub instead of a local generalist
hypothesis: If a specialized role that does not need broad cross-functional context, such as procurement, analytics or paid media, is hired in a lower-cost hub instead of as a local generalist, then the store gets comparable output at a lower fixed cost, because the arbitrage works for narrow specialist roles more reliably than for broad generalist ones.
does_not_apply_when: A role that needs broad, in-person, cross-functional context that a remote specialist hire would miss.

signal.check: A specialized, narrowly scoped role is currently filled or planned as a high-cost local generalist hire, with no comparison made against a specialist in a lower-cost hub.

expected_effect.size: source cites roughly $100k US versus $20,000 to $30,000 in Shenzhen and about $10,000 in the Philippines for comparable specialist work, as the source's own examples, not a current benchmark

risk.note: Verify current wage levels, visa and hiring realities for the target hub before committing; figures move over time.

prerequisites: A role clearly scoped as specialist rather than generalist
A hiring channel into the target lower-cost hub
steps: Map the open role as specialist or generalist based on how narrow its scope is.
If specialist, shortlist one or more lower-cost hubs with known talent in that specialty.
Benchmark current wage levels in the target hub against the local generalist hire cost.
Verify hiring, visa and time-zone realities before extending an offer.
Track output quality against the local-hire baseline for the first few months.

test.method: Compare output quality and cost per role for the offshore specialist hire against the local generalist alternative over the first quarter.
test.measure: Cost per role, output quality against the role's scorecard
test.read_point: At the end of the first quarter after the hire starts

title: Keep the store's proven marketing edge in-house below a revenue threshold
hypothesis: If a store below a set revenue size is winning specifically because of its own marketing skill, then keeping marketing in-house instead of outsourcing it to an agency protects that edge, because the source has rarely seen a founder who is genuinely good at marketing successfully delegate it before reaching very large scale.
does_not_apply_when: A store whose edge is product, not marketing skill, or one already past the scale where the source claims this holds.

signal.check: The store is winning mainly through marketing savviness, is below roughly $50 million in revenue, and is considering or already using an agency for its core marketing.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source states this as its own opinion and practice, not a measured comparison

risk.note: A staffing and structure decision, not a one-way commitment; an agency relationship can still be tested in parallel.

prerequisites: A clear, honest read on whether the store's edge is really marketing skill or product
steps: Diagnose honestly why the store is winning: a unique product, marketing skill, or both.
If marketing is the edge, keep the core marketing function in-house rather than handing it to an agency.
Give the in-house marketing lead direct control over the budget, since it is usually the largest controllable cost line.
If the edge is product rather than marketing, invest the same attention in product differentiation instead.
Revisit the decision as revenue scale changes, since the source ties this stance to a size range, not a permanent rule.

test.method: Compare performance on the same budget between the in-house team and an agency test on a limited slice of spend.
test.measure: roas_blended, cpa, time to iterate on creative or offers
test.read_point: After a full test cycle of at least one month per side

title: Run a deliberately lean headcount and add a role only at capacity
hypothesis: If the team stays deliberately lean and a new role is only added once the current team is visibly at capacity, then fixed cost stays lower and the resulting margin of error funds people and paid media instead of idle overhead, because hiring ahead of a proven need is what the source says erodes that margin.
does_not_apply_when: A team already understaffed to the point that delivery or service quality is visibly slipping.

signal.check: Headcount has been added ahead of a proven workload increase, or utilization across the team is consistently low.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source states this as its own opex-first policy, not a measured saving

risk.note: Pushed too far, a lean policy can hurt delivery, service levels or retention; watch for the seams the policy is meant to trigger on.

prerequisites: A way to see utilization across the current team
steps: Set a policy of not hiring ahead of a proven workload increase.
Watch for visible seams, such as missed deadlines or a role's owner consistently overloaded, as the hiring trigger.
Add specialist roles with clear utilization before adding broad generalist headcount.
Review the policy against delivery quality and team retention, not only against opex.
Adjust the threshold if the lean policy starts costing more in missed work than it saves in payroll.

test.method: Track opex per role and delivery or service metrics over two consecutive quarters under the lean-hiring policy.
test.measure: Opex per role, on-time delivery or SLA metrics, team retention
test.read_point: At the end of each quarter

title: Pre-brief top performers individually before a round of layoffs
hypothesis: If top performers are told individually, before a round of layoffs, that they are safe and the plan behind the cuts, then the layoff does not read to them as a signal to leave, because the source's own worst mistake was mass-cutting underperformers first and losing top people to the resulting panic.
does_not_apply_when: A single-person or very small team where individual pre-briefing and a formal layoff round are the same conversation.

signal.check: A round of layoffs or cuts is planned and no individual conversation with top performers has happened before the news becomes general.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source describes this as the fix for its own past mistake, not a measured result

risk.note: Once a layoff round is announced without this step, the trust cost of the surprise cannot be undone after the fact.

prerequisites: A clear list of who the top performers are
A firm plan for the cuts before any conversation happens
steps: Identify the team's top performers before finalizing who will be let go.
Meet each one individually, ahead of the general announcement.
Tell them plainly what is happening, why, and that they are safe.
Only after these conversations, carry out the planned cuts.
Follow through on any support promised to the people who stayed.

test.method: Track whether any top performer resigns in the 90 days after a layoff round where this step was used.
test.measure: Regretted attrition among top performers in the 90 days after the cuts
test.read_point: 90 days after the layoff round

title: Run continuous retention check-ins so a top performer never resigns as a surprise
hypothesis: If top performers get regular check-ins and are told about coming changes before they leak, not only during a crisis, then a resignation from a top performer stops being a surprise, because the source's own rule is that being blindsided by an A player leaving is itself evidence the retention work was not being done.
does_not_apply_when: A team small enough that daily contact with every person already covers this.

signal.check: A top performer's resignation has caught the store by surprise in the past, or no regular check-in rhythm exists with the people the store most needs to keep.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source states this as an ongoing discipline, not a measured result

risk.note: A recurring conversation habit; low cost, no downside if done honestly.

prerequisites: A named list of the team's top performers
steps: Identify who the store's top performers actually are.
Set a recurring check-in cadence with each of them, not only during a crisis.
Share coming changes with them before they become general news.
Ask directly how they are doing and whether anything is pulling them elsewhere.
Treat any surprise resignation from a top performer as a signal the check-in rhythm failed, and adjust it.

test.method: Track whether any top-performer resignation in a quarter was preceded by a recent check-in that missed the signal.
test.measure: Regretted attrition rate among top performers, check-in completion rate
test.read_point: Each quarter

title: Build a daily color-coded P&L digest with a required miss explanation
hypothesis: If a daily automated digest shows budget versus actual for revenue, spend and key metrics with a color for miss, beat and off-forecast, and the responsible owner must explain every miss in-thread, then problems surface and get owned the same day, because a weekly or monthly report leaves a miss unexplained for too long.
does_not_apply_when: A team too small for named metric owners to make the in-thread explanation step meaningful.

signal.check: Budget-versus-actual misses on revenue, spend or key metrics are only reviewed weekly or monthly, and no one is required to explain a miss when it happens.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source frames this as a compounding daily-improvement habit, not a measured result

risk.note: A reporting build only; does not itself change any budget or spend decision.

prerequisites: A budget or forecast per metric to compare actuals against
Named owners for each metric line
steps: List the P&L lines to track daily: revenue, ad spend, ROAS, repeat rate and any other key metric.
Set a budgeted or forecast value for each line to compare the actual against.
Build or automate a daily digest posted somewhere the whole team can see.
Color-code each line as a miss, a beat, or off-forecast.
Require the accountable owner to reply in-thread on any red line with the reason and the fix.
Flag any line that stays off-forecast for several days running and ask why the original forecast was wrong.

test.method: Track the time between a metric missing budget and the responsible owner posting an explanation, before and after the digest.
test.measure: Time to flag and explain a miss, number of misses with no logged explanation
test.read_point: After 4 weeks of the daily digest running

title: Run a daily task and time-log channel with every direct report
hypothesis: If every direct report posts their morning plan and an evening log of what got done and how time was spent, then a leader can spot overload or misplaced effort early, because a weekly or monthly check-in only shows the pattern after weeks of it have already happened.
does_not_apply_when: A team allergic to daily reporting overhead, where the logging itself becomes the biggest source of lost time.

signal.check: A team member's output looks off against a metric the daily P&L tracks, but there is no record of how their time was actually spent that week.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source gives no measured result, only its own operating practice

risk.note: This is a high-intensity, hands-on management style; it can read as micromanagement if not run consistently and predictably.

prerequisites: A messaging channel per direct report
Team buy-in that this is a support tool, not surveillance
steps: Create a personal channel for each direct report.
Have each person post their top 3 goals for the day each morning, plus the rest of their to-do list.
Have each person post what got done and a rough time breakdown each evening.
Cross-reference the time logs against the metrics that are off in the daily P&L digest.
Use the logs to decide who needs support, is overloaded, or is spending time on low-impact work.
Use the accumulated logs as a factual basis for periodic reviews instead of relying on memory.

test.method: Compare hours logged against impactful work versus low-impact work before and after adopting the channel.
test.measure: Share of logged hours on high-impact tasks, manager time spent identifying overload
test.read_point: After 4 to 6 weeks of daily logging

title: Give management feedback on a predictable daily cadence, not at random
hypothesis: If feedback to a junior team member is given on a predictable, daily cadence tied to a known system rather than randomly, then it trains faster without reading as micromanagement, because the source argues unstructured, unprompted feedback is what makes close oversight feel bad, not the frequency itself.
does_not_apply_when: A senior hire who needs autonomy more than a daily feedback loop.

signal.check: Feedback to junior team members is given only when something goes wrong and at unpredictable times, and it is read as micromanagement rather than coaching.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source presents this as its own contrarian management stance, not a measured result

risk.note: A management habit change; reversible at any time.

prerequisites: A daily reporting system, such as the P&L digest or task channel, to pair feedback against
steps: Set a fixed, known point in the day when feedback will be given, tied to an existing daily system.
Make the feedback specific to that day's numbers or task log, not a general critique.
Give it consistently, even when there is nothing negative to say.
Solicit feedback in the other direction too, so it is not one-way.
Hire and coach for a self-deprecating, gift-not-attack attitude toward feedback.

test.method: Track time to productivity and self-reported comfort with feedback for junior hires under this cadence versus prior ad hoc feedback.
test.measure: Time to productivity, junior team member retention
test.read_point: At 90 days for each new junior hire

title: Close the books monthly and dividend from free cash, not EBITDA
hypothesis: If the books close monthly, free cash flow is tracked separately from EBITDA, and working capital for planned growth is reserved before any distribution, then the owner takes out only cash that is genuinely free, because profit on paper is not the same as cash that can safely leave the business.
does_not_apply_when: A store with no management accounts yet; build that cadence first before this becomes possible.

signal.check: Distributions or owner draws are sized off EBITDA or a general profit feeling, with no monthly close and no working-capital reserve set aside first.

expected_effect.size: source projects taking about 65 to 75% of free cash flow out as distributions once the reserve is set, its own projection, not a benchmark

risk.note: Distributing before reserving working capital can starve the next order or ad push; get the reserve step right before automating anything.

prerequisites: Monthly management accounts covering revenue, COGS, opex and profit
steps: Close the books for the prior month by a fixed date, such as the 15th.
Calculate free cash flow separately from EBITDA for that month.
Estimate the working capital the coming months need for planned growth.
Only distribute what remains after that reserve.
Automate or pre-derive the process so the monthly distribution decision becomes routine.

test.method: Run the reserve-then-distribute process for 2 to 3 months and compare against prior EBITDA-based draws.
test.measure: cash_conversion_days, any cash shortfall in the following month's operations
test.read_point: After each monthly close

title: Use a five-slide accountability deck to negotiate a way out of a cash hole
hypothesis: If a short deck states the mistake plainly, explains the cause, lays out the recovery plan, gives a timeline and payback, then makes a specific ask, then a lender, partner or personal contact can price the risk and say yes faster, because the source's own experience is that a credible, short recovery story worked better than a long pitch.
does_not_apply_when: A situation needing a full investment process with a data room, not a personal or relationship-based ask.

signal.check: The store or its owner is trying to raise capital or renegotiate out of a cash shortfall and has no short, honest account of what happened and the plan to fix it.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source presents this as a personal turnaround story, not a measured outcome

risk.note: Building the deck itself carries no risk; the risk is in whatever deal it supports.
